title: Colts Would Be Better Off Trading Away Their Best Players
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts ' 26-20 loss to the Tennessee Titans on Sunday was more than another disappointing result in a season that has quickly gone off the rails. It was another reminder that the organization has spent years living in a constant state of mediocrity under general manager Chris Ballard .
Indianapolis entered the season with expectations of competing for a playoff spot. Instead, the Colts fell to 2-4 after surrendering a 13-point halftime lead to a Titans team that had yet to win a game. The loss exposed familiar problems, from a defense that struggled to pressure the quarterback to an offense that could not protect the football when it mattered most.
Ballard's tenure has run its course . He's had ample time to build a contender, yet Indy continues to fall short.
The Colts need a new direction, and that requires more than replacing the general manager. The organization must also be willing to move on from some of the players most closely associated with the current regime and give its next leadership group the resources to build a team of its own.
One of the biggest obstacles to a genuine rebuild is the temptation to preserve the core of the current roster. Indianapolis has several talented players who have earned their reputations around the league, but their individual accomplishments have not translated into the sustained team success the organization needs.
A new general manager should not be expected to inherit the same roster construction philosophy or feel obligated to preserve Ballard's most significant personnel investments. The next regime needs the freedom to determine which players fit its vision and which assets would be better used elsewhere.
Keeping the same core together simply because those players are talented would risk prolonging the very cycle the Colts need to escape. Ownership must recognize that continuity is not inherently valuable when it continues to produce the same disappointing results.
The frustration inside the locker room is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore. Following Sunday's loss, defensive tackle DeForest Buckner expressed his exhaustion with the team's recurring shortcomings.
"I'm sick and tired of the same song and dance every year."
Buckner's words capture the frustration of not just a player, but a fanbase that has experienced the highs and lows of the Colts' recent seasons without seeing the organization take a meaningful step forward. Players like Buckner have invested years of their careers into trying to make Indianapolis a contender. They shouldn't have to waste the rest of their playing days waiting for the organization to figure out how to get there.
#Colts DT DeForest Buckner’s postgame presser. “I’m sick and tired of the same song and dance every year.” pic.twitter.com/0lwXhKDpVS
The Colts need to stop treating the current roster as something that must be preserved at all costs. A new regime deserves the opportunity to evaluate the team on its own terms, and several of Indianapolis' best players could be better served by continuing their careers elsewhere.
Recouping draft capital should be one of Indianapolis' top priorities moving forward . The franchise needs more opportunities to add young talent, address roster weaknesses and give its next general manager the resources to build a sustainable contender.
Buckner and Quenton Nelson are the clearest candidates to move. Both are foundational players who have spent years establishing themselves among the league's best at their respective positions. Both are also playing on contracts that expire after the 2026 season, putting the Colts at risk of losing two valuable assets without receiving anything in return, but that also gives Indy's trade partner the freedom to sign their new addition to a fresh contract instead of inheriting one they did not negotiate.
If the organization is ready to move on from Ballard and acknowledge that the current roster has not delivered, holding onto two veteran stars on expiring deals makes little sense. Indianapolis can recoup draft capital, give the next regime additional resources and allow two accomplished players to join teams with clearer paths to contention.
The Colts should not stop there, though the decisions become more complicated and difficult.
Jonathan Taylor remains one of the most important pieces of the offense. Cornerback Sauce Gardner is a young, established talent in the secondary, while defensive end Laiatu Latu still has room to develop into a cornerstone of the pass rush. All three could help establish a competitive floor for the next regime, giving a new coaching staff a foundation to build around rather than forcing it to restart from scratch.
A reset doesn't have to become a full teardown, and Indianapolis should not sacrifice every established player for the sole purpose of accruing draft capital---that would be reckless. A new general manager needs talented players who can contribute while younger prospects develop.
But Taylor, Gardner and Latu should not be untouchable. Taylor's contract and the market for running backs would factor into any potential deal. Gardner's age and established reputation, plus consideration to the fact he hasn't been a Colt for very long, could attract a contender looking for a top cornerback. Latu's youth and potential could appeal to a team seeking a long-term answer off the edge.
The Colts need to actively explore the market for all three. If they receive a trade package that would meaningfully improve its long-term outlook, the organization shouldn't hesitate make the deal.
Keeping a player simply because he is talented or was acquired through a significant investment would repeat the same mistake of prioritizing past decisions over future needs.
The distinction is straightforward: Buckner and Nelson should be moved because of their contract situations. Taylor, Gardner and Latu can help provide a foundation for the new regime, but their value in a trade must be weighed against what they could contribute to a rebuilt roster.
The goal  is simple: give the next regime as much flexibility as possible to build a winner .
Trading away established talent is not an easy path forward. Draft picks are uncertain, rebuilding takes time and a new general manager could make mistakes of their own. Indianapolis would also have to replace the production and leadership of players who have been central to the roster for years.
But the alternative is to keep trying the same approach year after year and hope the results eventually change. And we've already seen how that story goes.
Indianapolis has spent years trying to find its way back to the postseason and establish itself as a consistent contender. Sunday's loss to Tennessee was another painful indication that the franchise has not reached that standard. The organization can't keep asking its players and fans for patience while making the same decisions that have left it in this position.
Buckner and Nelson deserve the opportunity to compete for something meaningful during what remains of their primes. The same is true of Taylor, Gardner and Latu if the Colts cannot offer them a credible path toward winning football. These players have invested their careers in Indianapolis, and the organization owes them an honest assessment of where the franchise is headed.
Moving on from Ballard and trading Buckner and Nelson would give the Colts a clear starting point. Exploring the market for Taylor, Gardner and Latu would give the next regime additional options without requiring a complete teardown.
The Colts have reached a point where preserving the status quo is the greater risk. A new-look front office needs the authority to shape its own roster, the draft capital to address its weaknesses and the freedom to make decisions based on the future, not the past.
Indianapolis can't change what happened on Sunday, but it can control how they react. By making big decisions, ownership can indicate they're willing to do…

title: Colts Reach Rock Bottom in Chris Ballard's Magnum Opus
full_text:
The sense of urgency for head coach Shane Steichen and longtime general manager Chris Ballard has never been higher - or at least that's what Indianapolis Colts ' Owner/CEO Carlie Irsay-Gordon said ahead of the 2026 regular season.
But after six weeks of play, the Colts look like the same uninspired team that's served as a revolving door of mediocrity under Chris Ballard's reign.
The Indianapolis Colts have posted new lows each season under Ballard and Co., but their Week 6 loss to the winless Tennessee Titans was so inexcusable that it should be the final nail in this regime's coffin.
This roster is likely beyond saving, but there's still a chance the season can be salvaged. The only way that hypothetical becomes feasible is if wholesale changes are made before the season concludes.
The Indianapolis Colts were up 13-0 against the Tennessee Titans at halftime, but 20 unanswered points opened the door for the worst team in the league to rebound, and Shane Steichen's team refused to close it shut.
This loss in question could be viewed as a one-off performance that a playoff contender just needs to shake off, but the optics around Indy's already bleak outlook suggest the opposite: the Colts may have lost to the team with the worst record in the NFL, but they themselves are closer to being the worst team.
The Colts allowed just 189 total yards of offense, and more than doubled up with offensive production of their own with 399 yards produced, but they still managed to leave their home field with a loss.
Shane Steichen's Colts offense is thoroughly broken.
Quarterback Daniel Jones has officially reverted to his New York Giants self, one of the league's top offensive lines looks uncharacteristically lost more often than not, the run game cannot be relied on to save the day, and the passing attack is nonexistent.
The offense's firepower is lacking, especially from its passcatchers, but there's no excuse worthy of absolving Steichen and Co. of their offensive sins.
But Lou Anarumo's Colts defense has not been much better, either.
The Colts have the worst pass rush in the entire NFL, their secondary has solid coverage defenders but lacks playmakers, and their linebacker room is littered with subpar options.
No matter how you shake it, the Indianapolis Colts are officially a dumpster fire.
Even more so, they very well may be the league's new laughingstock.
There are unfortunately plenty of examples to compare this loss to, but considering they are supposed to serve as lessons to his reign, Indianapolis' Week 6 loss to the Titans looks to be Chris Ballard's Magnum Opus.
Entering the 2025 regular season, a poll done by The Athletic showed that Indianapolis Colts fans are the least excited fanbase among all teams in the NFL.
An unforeseen historic start to that season briefly changed everyone's tune, but a mid-season implosion reminded folks that Chris Ballard's Colts may just be destined for mediocrity after all.
Fast forward one calendar year, and things looked even bleaker entering a new season.
Chris Ballard, Shane Steichen, and Co. hitched their wagon to an Achilles-torn Daniel Jones, banked on DeForest Buckner returning to form despite suffering a serious neck injury, and looked to replicate their offensive success from the season prior by signing an ankle-recovering Alec Pierce to a historic free agent deal.
The outlook remained uninspired; therefore, Colts fans checked out as they awaited the inevitable demise of the Ballard era.
But what we've witnessed through six weeks is grounds for a mid-season fire sale.
As long as fans keep showing up, the Colts have no problem staying the course, but that's not the case anymore.
Not only are Colts fans not filling up Lucas Oil Stadium anymore, they're booing more consistently and loudly than ever before, and season ticket holders are actively trying to encourage fellow members to forego renewals for the foreseeable future.
This fanbase has become numb to such disappointment, and can you blame them?
There's an incredibly fair reason that Indianapolis Colts fans were caught chanting "Fire Ballard!" at the tail end of the team's embarrassing loss at home to the 0-5 Tennessee Titans.
The Colts should have parted ways with Chris Ballard at numerous stops throughout his tenure, but if there's been any time to do so during the middle of a season, it's now.
We've predicted this season will finally be Ballard's last stand, but perhaps now's the best time to rip off the band-aid.
Ridding oneself of the mediocrity that the Ballard era has normalized is a good start for changing one's own scenery, but an exodus of the roster's top players should be the next step.
The Colts need to set up their next regime as best they can, so dealing assets to recoup for the incoming era is the top priority.
Indianapolis is already without a first-round pick for the upcoming NFL Draft after new ownership allowed Ballard to dish out multiple top draft selections for cornerback Sauce Gardner at the 2025 trade deadline.
The Colts would benefit from parting ways with key players Jonathan Taylor, Quenton Nelson, DeForest Buckner, and Sauce Gardner, but moving on from the man who's tied to them is the first order of business.
Parting ways with Chris Ballard would allow the Colts to begin their rebuild early, while also giving them an (albeit unlikely) chance to rebound in the ongoing season.
In theory, immediately shipping out your best players would make the current outlook even bleaker; however, the Colts have proven time and time again that no matter what the roster looks like, success is impossible so long as Chris Ballard lurks behind the scenes.
The pillars of the Colts' roster have not gotten the job done, so there's no reason to believe they'll unlock a new version of themselves anytime soon.
If parting ways with Chris Ballard is not an option at this point in time, doing so with head coach Shane Steichen would be the next best thing.
Someone needs to be held accountable, so if it's not Ballard, then the man leading the charge on the field should be the one to go.
Both Steichen and Ballard experiments have run their course in Indianapolis, so ideally both are let go; however, if a full-blown fire sale and/or Ballard's departure isn't in the cards, Steichen should see the door.
Special teams coordinator Brian Mason and Assistant General Manager Ed Dodds feel like the ideal interim replacements, but we'll have to see if any changes are even on the table first.
One playoff victory, zero divisional titles, and countless examples of redefining what it means to hit rock bottom across an entire decade have become what's expected of Chris Ballard's reign.
When will enough be enough?
Noah Compton is the Publisher of Indianapolis Colts On SI. Noah is from the Indy area and has been covering the Colts since 2022, including stops at FanSided, The Blue Stable, and SBNation.

title: Why Colts Should (Finally) Part Ways With GM Chris Ballard
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts find themselves in a rare opportunity where it makes sense to part ways with their general manager mid-season.
After a decade of disappointment, Colts ownership decided to run it back once and for all, suggesting that this time, Chris Ballard and Co. must win the AFC South and/or make the playoffs to right the ship.
Just six weeks into the 2026 regular season, it's evident that this sinking ship cannot be saved. Even more, the ship has already sunk to the bottom of the sea.
The Colts sit at a lowly 2-4 record after losing to the 0-5 Tennessee Titans at home, and this unforgivable loss should be enough to take the keys from the man who is responsible for constructing such an unacceptable, near-disrespectful product year in and year out.
The staff and rosters have not held up their end of the bargain throughout the years, but each shortcoming can be attributed to and traced back to general manager Chris Ballard's decision-making.
Furthermore, this most recent implosion is the perfect culmination of what the Ballard era has been: a revolving door of mediocrity.
But if Colts ownership has already planned to cut ties with this regime following the season if they cannot produce results, why would they jump the gun and do so now?
The Colts should have ended the Ballard era on numerous occasions throughout his tenure, most recently, ahead of this season, but there's no longer any reason to keep this regime around.
The current coaching staff, led by head coach Shane Steichen, defensive coordinator Lou Anarumo, offensive coordinator Jim Bob Cooter, and special teams coordinator Brian Mason, will also likely see the door after the season, but there's an argument to be made that you'd rather keep them around and part ways with Chris Ballard, as opposed to having a full-blown fire sale.
The roster and staff are what they are. There's more than likely no chance any version of this team rebounds this season, but seeing what a Colts team looks like without Chris Ballard lurking behind the scenes could be enough to inspire some confidence moving forward, at least as far as this season goes.
Eliminating the common denominator could very well be enough to get the Colts' swagger back, but there's a more important factor at play.
Parting ways with general manager Chris Ballard not only allows the Colts to get a brief audition period of what they've got, but more importantly, it also gives them a golden opportunity to sell off their best assets as they prepare for the next era.
Ideally, both Ballard and head coach Shane Steichen are relieved of their duties and we get a truly fresh look at what this roster can do, but if nothing else, the former should see the door.
The product we've gotten after a decade of roster construction is not only not good enough, but it's destroyed the fanbase's will to live.
With one playoff victory, zero divisional titles, and no future to look forward to after a decade of disappointment, how can you blame them?
The apathy is loud, so ridding oneself of this normalized mediocrity should be step one in the pursuit of earning the fanbase's trust back, and that starts with ripping off the band-aid that Chris Ballard has so regularly replaced.
The Indianapolis Colts would likely turn to longtime assistant general manager Ed Dodds in the scenario that Chris Ballard is fired mid-season.
While most may view Ballard's and Dodds' inherent ties as a reason to part ways with the entire front office, Dodds has been regarded as one of the NFL's top general manager candidates for quite some time now, and it's been shocking that he's stuck around to remain Ballard's right-hand man after going through numerous interviews with interested teams across the league.
Dodds would likely jump at the opportunity to become a first-time general manager, even if that means in an interim capacity.
Ideally, the Colts ownership trio of Carlie Irsay-Gordon, Kalen Jackson, and Casey Foyt turns to Dodds mid-season, and they instruct him to deal any assets they have remaining in an attempt to recoup as much draft capital as possible for the next regime.
Of course, Dodds may not appreciate the notion that he's to take his friend's job and rectify the damage they've done so that the next guy can benefit from it, but again, it's one of 32 jobs in the world.
I'm sure even Ballard would tell Dodds to jump at the opportunity, but that aside, the top priority moving forward is to set up the next era with the best possible situation.
The Colts are famously without their 2027 first-round pick after Chris Ballard traded away a blockbuster haul for cornerback Sauce Gardner at the 2025 trade deadline, so Indianapolis is already set for an uphill climb when it comes to attracting top general manager candidates.
Maximizing their outlook for 2027 and beyond is what should be the primary focus moving forward.
The Colts' 2026 season is already lost. They'll need a miracle to suggest otherwise.
Given how unlikely it is that Indianapolis rebounds and makes any noise in the playoffs, the best course of action from here on out is to think of the future.
Every decision from this point on should be trying to answer the question, "Does this make future us better?"
To do that, the Colts must focus on adding as much top draft capital as possible, and that begins with shopping their best players ahead of the NFL Trade Deadline, which is scheduled for Tuesday, November 10th at 4:00 PM EST.
There are no untouchable players on the roster anymore. Some definitely deserve the designation; however, this regime has made it impossible to consider anyone as a long-term option.
Whoever ends up calling the shots in the post-Ballard hypothetical should entertain any call that comes asking about Jonathan Taylor, Quenton Nelson, DeForest Buckner, Sauce Gardner, or Laiatu Latu.
Taylor, Gardner, and Latu are all under contract for 2027 and/or beyond, so the Colts could very well choose to keep them around to become the next regime's pillar players, though that should only happen if strong deals aren't offered.
However, when it comes to Nelson and Buckner, it'd almost be malpractice not to trade them elsewhere.
Both players are on expiring deals and will become unrestricted free agents this coming offseason. This added layer would do wonders come negotiation time, given that a true Super Bowl contender would jump at the opportunity to go all-in by trading draft capital for a one-year rental.
Legitimate contenders are worried about the present, while the Colts should be focused on the future.
The Colts have an opportunity to sell their best players to the highest bidder, and the fact that interested suitors could use this to not only bolster their current roster, but also figure out a long-term extension to get ahead of free agency and lock down their newcomer for the long haul would favor the Colts in negotiations.
Again, not a single player on the Colts' roster should be deemed untouchable moving forward.
This team has featured these talented players for each of their annual implosions, so there's no reason to believe they'll figure it out anytime soon.
It's clear the 2026 Colts won't be making the noise come postseason play, so ensuring a healthy transition should be the top priority from here on out.
This season may not be salvageable, but the future is.
Noah Compton is the Publisher of Indianapolis Colts On SI. Noah is from the Indy area and has been covering the Colts since 2022, including stops at FanSided, The Blue Stable, and SBNation.

title: The Good, the Bad & the Unforgivable from the Colts’ Embarrassing Week 6 Loss
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts faced off against a floundering Tennessee Titans team on Sunday that was still looking for its first win of the season.
For the 2-3 Colts, it was an opportunity to take care of business against one of the league’s basement dwellers and pick up their second AFC South win of the season.
Instead, Indianapolis stumbled its way to a 26-20 defeat, falling to 2-4 in a season where anything less than a playoff appearance is unacceptable.
Fans showered the team with boos as the clock expired. Some broke out in chants, demanding accountability from the team officials responsible for the current state of mediocrity the franchise is stuck in. After surrendering a 13-point halftime lead to a division rival that had yet to win a game, the Colts gave their fans plenty of reasons to be frustrated.
Here’s a look at the good, the bad and the straight up unforgivable from Indianapolis’ latest defeat.
The Colts passing game was without starting tight end Tyler Warren for the first time since drafting Warren two years ago. The overall production suffered without his presence, but the rest of the tight end depth chart stepped up in a big way.
Mo Alie-Cox caught the first Colts’ touchdown of the game and filled his usual run blocking role, helping the offense rush for 165 yards as a unit. Will Mallory made his season debut after spending the first five weeks on injured reserve with a thumb injury as well, catching two of his six targets for 20 yards.
The void left by Warren wasn’t filled entirely—it’s almost impossible to make up for his absence—but the Colts still got some solid play out of the guys who stepped up to replace him.
Although they couldn’t maintain their excellent start in the second half, the Colts defense played a strong first two quarters. Tennessee was held scoreless at the half, threw an interception and was limited to just 64 total yards.
Of course, the second half looked much different. Indianapolis surrendered 20 unanswered points, scoring on all five possessions, and gave up no sacks to an invisible Indianapolis pass rush.
Even though they couldn’t sustain their success, the Colts defense showed they could shut down an offense, albeit one of the league’s worst, making their first half showing one of the few bright spots from an otherwise dark Sunday afternoon.
Where would the Colts be without Jonathan Taylor?
Even while surrounded by total mediocrity, Taylor’s individual brilliance continues to shine through. The Colts superstar running back recorded 151 yards from scrimmage against the Titans, the most of his season so far, and added a touchdown late to keep the Colts in the game. The only blemish on his statline was a lost fumble in the second half.
In ten career games against Tennessee, Taylor is now up to 1,054 total scrimmage yards, over 105 yards per game. Seems like Taylor might have the franchise’s number.
One of the few strengths of the Colts roster as it currently looks is the offensive line. The unit is widely considered one of the best starting groups in the league.
But if you watched Sunday’s game, they looked nothing like the elite unit they’re meant to be.
The Colts offensive line particularly struggled in pass protection. Daniel Jones was sacked six times, more than the previous two weeks combined.
Tennessee attacked Indy’s edges, and Jalen Travis struggled at right tackle. Without Tyler Warren to help chip rushers on his way out to run his route, the Titans had more one-on-one opportunities, and took advantage.
The rushing game did manage 165 yards, but that number is irrelevant in the larger context. The offensive line simply wasn’t up to the task, which is inexcusable when the opponent is winless.
The Colts’ special teams unit allowed several big plays, quite uncharacteristically.
On the first play of the fourth quarter, Tennessee’s Chimere Dike returned a Rigoberto Sanchez punt 58 yards to help set up a short field, which Cam Ward and the Titans offense capitalized on with a four-play drive to tie the game at 13.
The very next drive, the Colts punt team made another huge mistake, but this one was bigger.
Tennessee managed to block Sanchez’s punt and scoop up the loose ball, which was run back for a touchdown that put the Titans up 20-13 late in the fourth quarter.
Blocked punt leads to a scoop and score by the defense‼️ 📺: @NFLonFOX pic.twitter.com/t6MOCAauY8
Indianapolis’ special teams unit, which typically is very reliable, simply had a bad day at the worst possible time. Frustrating scenes.
Indianapolis held Tennessee to just 185 yards of total offense, yet lost by six. The difference? Field position.
The Titans average starting field position on Sunday was their own 35-yard line. That’s a full seven yards further up the field from the Colts, who started at their own 28-yard line on average.
Taylor’s fumble and the long punt return from Dike were major difference makers, as each allowed the Titans to start on the other side of midfield. They took advantage of their short fields, turning each opportunity into points.
The Colts already have plenty to clean up across the board. If they’re incapable of winning the field position battle, what are they capable of winning?
After cleaning up many of his turnover issues last season, Daniel Jones is back to his old self.
Jones’ two interceptions against Tennessee brought his season total to nine turnovers. For comparison, he had 11 in 13 games a season ago. As a result, Indianapolis now possesses a -8 turnover differential, the worst in the league.
In his defense, Jones wasn’t the primary player responsible for the first interception. As Jones scrambled to his right looking to extend a broken play, he tried hitting Josh Downs for a gain of about five yards. But, he put too much zip on the throw, which bounced off Downs’ hands and into the arms of Amani Hooker.
Amani with an incredible interception 📺: @NFLonFOX pic.twitter.com/wkm4jCgZdo
But that’s where the excuses stop for Jones. He continues to put the ball in harm's way, despite knowing so, and it’s hurting the Colts tremendously. Simply inexcusable, especially in a season where the pressure to win is well and truly on.
Josh Downs is no stranger to drops. The fourth-year receiver has 14 in his first three seasons, and they were an issue again against the Titans.
Downs had two major drops in the game. One bounced off his hands and to Tennessee for an interception while the other halted the offense’ momentum late in the game as they looked to pull off a late comeback.
Considering the injury issues the Colts have at wide out, Downs hasn’t taken advantage of his chance to separate himself as a go-to option for Jones.
And without Tyler Warren, who’s the Colts best weapon in the passing game? If today was any indication, until Downs cleans up his drop problem, it certainly won’t be him.
New week, same story. The Colts pass rush was nowhere to be found. Again.
As a unit, the Indianapolis defense recorded no sacks and just a single QB hit on Cam Ward. Tennessee has done a good job this season of keeping their quarterback clean this season (just 10 sacks allowed, T-6th fewest in the league), but the effort shown by the Colts was laughably poor.
The only play that made any sort of an impact was the lone quarterback hit on Ward. Andetomiwa Adebawore got pressure in his face and forced a bad throw, which wound up in the hands of Cam Bynum for Indy’s only turnover of the day.
Through six games, it’s obvious the Colts didn’t do enough to bolster their pass rush in the offseason. Missing out on Trey Hendrickson definitely didn’t help, but the franchise’s contingency plan there wasn’t good enough.
And in a game where the opposition pass rush gets to the quarterback six times, putting up a zero, especially with so much on the line this season, is downright dreadful. Indy’s pass rush hasn’t recorded a sack since the third quarter of last week’s loss to the Steelers, a streak that speaks volumes to how badly the defensive line…

title: Colts vs. Titans Best Bets: Follow the Trends in Week 6
full_text:
Through five weeks, we’re 11-3 on Colts props and 12-11 overall. We’ve got a pretty good pulse on this Indianapolis offense, and we’re looking to keep climbing further into the plus column.
With Ashton Dulin out, Alec Pierce on IR and Tyler Warren questionable, Indianapolis should lean heavily on Jonathan Taylor. However, Tennessee ranks eighth in both run defense and tackling grades via PFF, making this matchup tougher than it looks.
Taylor has scored three touchdowns in each of his last three meetings with Tennessee, and his ability to control the game could dictate how nearly every prop on this card plays out.
Let's get into my five best bets for Sunday.
Tennessee has scored just 58 points through five games, the fewest in football, while allowing only 109, the ninth fewest in football.
Daniel Jones has thrown just three touchdown passes this season, and with Indianapolis’ receiving corps depleted, I expect Shane Steichen to lean on Taylor and try to control this game.
Even if the Colts put a decent amount of points on the board, I don’t trust Tennessee’s offense enough to push this total over.
Taylor has cleared this number in three of his last four games, with the only miss coming last week when Pittsburgh held him to 15 carries for 45 yards.
He is averaging 20.2 carries per game and has a 29-carry performance against Tennessee on his résumé. With the passing attack this thin, I expect Indianapolis to get Taylor involved early and often.
I’ve said it all season: we’re riding this line until the wheels fall off. Shrader has cleared it in four straight games, is 16-for-16 on field goals this season and just drilled five against Pittsburgh.
This offense continues to stall enough in scoring territory to give him opportunities. Until the books force us off it, I’m staying right here.
Pollard has cleared 12.5 yards on his longest rush in four of five games this season and eight of his last 10.
Indianapolis has allowed the fifth-most yards per carry to running backs, and Pollard’s interior-heavy rushing style attacks one of the weakest areas of this Colts defense.
I like his chances of breaking off at least one substantial run against Indianapolis.
Ayomanor has cleared this line in seven of his last 10 games and in both career matchups against Indianapolis, finishing with 38 and 52 yards in those meetings.
The Colts secondary remains attackable, and at just 15.5 yards, one decent completion can nearly cash this by itself.
This entire card revolves around Taylor. If he controls the game, the under gets a boost, Shrader should keep seeing chances and Tennessee’s overall volume shrinks.
Good luck, and bet responsibly.

title: Colts Could Be Without Key Offensive Weapon Against Titans
full_text:
Friday brought a mixed bag of injury news for the Indianapolis Colts ahead of Sunday's AFC South matchup with the Tennessee Titans.
Several key players appear to be trending in the right direction, but Indianapolis has already ruled out two contributors, and rookie tight end Tyler Warren remains questionable.
Of all the developments on Friday's report, Warren's status is easily the one that concerns me most.
Warren was arguably the only bright spot for this offense in last week's 34-22 loss to Pittsburgh, catching seven passes for 83 yards and adding a one-yard rushing touchdown.
Through five games, he has 30 catches for 213 yards and two touchdowns, trailing only Josh Downs in receiving yards for Indianapolis. Losing him would be a massive blow to a passing attack that is already running out of healthy weapons.
Alec Pierce remains on injured reserve, Darius Slayton was released Friday without ever appearing in a game for Indianapolis, and Dulin has now been ruled out for a second straight week.
That leaves Keenan Allen, Josh Downs, Laquon Treadwell and Deion Burks as the primary wide receiver options, with Warren's status potentially making things even thinner.
Warren wasn't listed on the injury report Wednesday or Thursday, making his late-week appearance with a groin injury even more concerning.
The good news is Allen and Downs have logged two straight full practices after lighter workloads Wednesday. Daniel Jones was also a full participant all three days despite remaining on the report with an ankle designation.
Will Mallory practiced fully all week as he works his way back from a thumb injury, although he is also listed as questionable while Indianapolis decides whether to activate him from injured reserve.
Outside of Warren, Carlies and Dulin, Friday was fairly encouraging.
Jonathan Taylor logged his second consecutive full practice, while Jalen Travis progressed from not practicing Wednesday to limited Thursday and full participation Friday.
Grover Stewart returned to full participation after a rest day Thursday, while Charvarius Ward has now practiced fully on back-to-back days. DeForest Buckner did not practice Friday, but his absence was rest-related.
Carlies being out for a second straight week still hurts a linebacker room that has struggled early this season, but Warren's status carries the biggest offensive implications.
Tennessee owns PFF's 26th-ranked coverage unit through five weeks, which should give Indianapolis an opportunity to attack through the air.
But without Pierce, Dulin and potentially Warren, I am not sure the Colts have enough firepower to fully take advantage. That could put even more pressure on Downs and Taylor.
Tennessee ranks eighth in both PFF run-defense grade and tackling grade, meaning the matchup on the ground may be tougher than its 0-5 record suggests.
With Indianapolis' bottom ranked pass defense, both teams may want to attack through the air.
With an already depleted receiving corps, having Warren available could be the difference between an offense that finds its rhythm and another frustrating afternoon for Daniel Jones.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: 3 Most Important Things Colts’ Shane Steichen Said Ahead of Week 6
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts will look to get back to .500 on Sunday when they host the Tennessee Titans in an AFC South matchup. Indianapolis has several areas to clean up as it looks to maintain its position in the division and continue building toward its goals.
Ahead of the game, head coach Shane Steichen addressed the media to discuss the team's preparation and what the Colts need to do to put together a complete performance against Tennessee. Here are three of the most important takeaways from his comments.
The Colts have received inconsistent production from their wide receivers in recent weeks, and opposing defenses are beginning to adjust to their most productive targets. Heading into Sunday's matchup with the Titans, head coach Shane Steichen knows the offense must find ways to counter those adjustments.
One challenge has been getting Josh Downs involved when defenses focus on taking him away, particularly on third downs. Steichen acknowledged the attention Downs has received and explained how Indianapolis hopes to respond.
“Yeah I mean, each and every week we’ve got to be prepared for what defenses do to him," Steichen said. "They're doubling him on third down a few times...we’ve got to do a great job of moving him around to get him freed up when teams are doing that because he is a hell of a player."
When defenses take away the first option, Steichen said the Colts must capitalize on opportunities elsewhere in the passing game, saying they're always looking for new ways to get their playmakers the ball.
Indianapolis could also have another option as it looks for more production from its receivers. The Colts recently added Quez Watkins, who could provide a vertical threat if he earns a role against Tennessee. Steichen was noncommittal about whether Watkins would make his debut this week.
Steichen identified turnovers as a major area of emphasis for the Colts heading into Sunday's matchup with the Titans. Indianapolis is -6 in turnover differential, tied for worst in the league.
Steichen said this week that taking the ball away, as well as protecting it, were the main points of emphasis in this week's preparation for Tennessee.
“Obviously, you got – you preach it, but you got to practice it like crazy," he said. "It's got to be all day, every day in practice. You can't talk about it. You got to go do it.”
The message is clear: Indianapolis has to improve on both sides of the turnover equation.
With the AFC South matchup approaching, the Colts will look to turn that emphasis in practice into results on Sunday. As Steichen made clear, stressing the importance of turnovers is not enough. Indianapolis must execute when it matters.
Jonathan Taylor has remained a productive part of the Colts' offense, but Indianapolis has yet to create the explosive runs that have made Taylor so dangerous throughout his career. Ahead of Sunday's matchup with the Titans, Steichen acknowledged that getting those game-changing plays back into the offense is an area the team needs to address.
“Obviously, the chunk plays like we saw last year, we haven't had those in the run game, and it'd be great to get back to that and get those explosives going forward,” Steichen said.
Steichen pointed to both scheme and execution as factors in creating more opportunities for Taylor, who hasn't recorded a run of 25 yards or more in over 570 snaps. Indianapolis has to adjust to the defensive fronts it faces each week while making sure its players execute when the offense gets the looks it wants.
“Execution's got to be at a premium.," Steichen said.
Taylor's ability to turn routine carries into explosive gains can add another dimension to the Colts' offense. Against Tennessee, Indianapolis will look to create the conditions for those bigger plays and give its star running back more opportunities to break through.

title: Colts Pull Plug on Darius Slayton Experiment: Is a Corresponding Move Coming?
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts have released wide receiver Darius Slayton, the team announced, ending a bizarre month-long stint with the team.
We have released WR Darius Slayton.
The Colts signed Slayton on Sept. 22 in an attempt to remedy their injury problems. The idea was that Slayton would reconnect with a former teammate Daniel Jones to help stabilize the passing game until the Colts returned to full strength.
Less than a month later, Slayton is out of Indianapolis without having appeared in any of the four games he was available for.
Indianapolis caught the injury bug early in the season at wide receiver. Alec Pierce suffered an ankle injury in Week 2, Ashton Dulin has been navigating a hamstring injury and Keenan Allen has dealt with a few bumps and bruises, missing the game in London.
Pierce’s absence left a huge void in the Colts passing game, taking away their best field-stretching deep threat. He had established himself as one of the NFL's most productive downfield receivers, leading the league in yards per reception in both 2024 and 2025. With Pierce expected to miss several weeks and Dulin also dealing with an injury, the Colts needed another option capable of stretching the field.
Slayton offered a potential solution to both problems. The seven-year veteran averaged 15.0 yards per catch across his time with the New York Giants and already had an established connection with Daniel Jones, having played alongside the quarterback for six seasons. Indianapolis was betting that chemistry and Slayton's downfield ability could help keep the passing game afloat until Pierce returned.
The move made sense on paper, but the Colts never got to see whether Slayton could deliver. He was inactive for his first two games with Indianapolis while learning the offense, then appeared to be nearing his debut before a knee injury sidelined him against Pittsburgh last week.
Why Slayton Never Saw the Field
After signing with the Colts on a Tuesday, Slayton had a short week to get up to speed. Ultimately, he couldn’t learn the offense in time, leading to Indianapolis making him a healthy scratch in Week 3. Head coach Shane Steichen pointed to that adjustment period when explaining Slayton's initial absence, saying he needed to continue developing and growing within the offense.
It’s a similar story for the following week against Washington. Slayton wasn’t quite up to speed just yet, so he spent another week as a healthy inactive, though questions began to arise. Slayton was expected to play a valuable role, but hadn’t yet touched the field.
Things were trending in the right direction for Slayton to make his Colts debut in Pittsburgh. But in Indy’s final practice before the game, Slayton picked up a knee injury and was ruled out. He returned to full practice Wednesday, putting him back in contention to play, but the Colts released him just two days later.
What’s Next for the Colts?
Slayton's departure leaves Indianapolis right back where it started four weeks ago, without a field-stretching vertical threat. Strangely, Slayton never made it onto the field despite the team's need, and Indianapolis has opted to move on rather than continue waiting for him to be ready.
One player who could benefit from the decision is rookie Deion Burks. The seventh-round pick has seen limited opportunities through the first five games of his career, but with Slayton no longer in the picture, Burks could have a chance to earn a larger role.
The Colts are also waiting for Alec Pierce to return from injured reserve, which could eventually provide the downfield threat they hoped Slayton would supply. Pierce is eligible to return for Indianapolis' Week 7 matchup against the Minnesota Vikings on Oct. 25, and the release of Slayton indicates Pierce could be progressing rapidly towards an earlier return than expected.
Until Pierce is healthy enough to play, Indianapolis will need its other receivers to find ways to fill the void. The Colts explored a potential trade for Marvin Harrison Jr. before missing out on the former Arizona Cardinals receiver, leaving the team to consider other options as the trade deadline approaches. Several potential trade targets could help address that need, but Slayton's departure leaves Indianapolis still searching for a solution.

title: Colts Must Win These 3 Matchups If They Want to Beat Titans in Week 6
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts are fresh off an all-too-familiar loss to the Steelers in Pittsburgh.
The Colts are 2-3 entering their Week 6 AFC South matchup against the Tennessee Titans, their second divisional game of the young season and first time taking on the Titans.
Tennessee is off a lowly 0-5 start to the 2026 season, and now aims to march into Lucas Oil Stadium on Sunday and get its first win against a divisional rival.
The winless Titans beating the Colts in Week 6 would almost be poetic, given that it would assist the ongoing train wreck that is led by conductor Chris Ballard.
The Colts desperately need to start stacking wins if they want any shot at the division and/or playoffs, and I'm breaking down the three ways they can almost guarantee a much-needed victory against the Titans in Week 6.
Colts' star running back Jonathan Taylor has had a strong start to the season, but he's itching for a breakout game, and what better time than at home against a divisional opponent in the Tennessee Titans?
Taylor is ninth in rushing yards (398) and T-fourth in rushing touchdowns (6), but his career-low 3.9 yards per carry (previous low is 4.4 ypc) screams breakout game.
And the Colts are desperate to lean on Taylor, as their passing offense has become unreliable .
Where the Colts may specifically be able to beat the Titans on the ground is through gap scheme runs, with Taylor's recent success suggesting it's sustainable.
Jonathan Taylor has rushed for a league-high 139 yards on gap scheme runs this season, including five explosive runs (10+ yards), tied for the most among running backs, according to Next Gen Stats. More via NGS:
Taylor has also forced eight missed tackles on gap scheme runs this season, tied for the third-most among backs. Since the start of the 2025 season, Taylor leads the league in gap-scheme rushing yards (726), touchdowns (13), and missed tackles forced (43).
Rushing for 2+ touchdowns in three of his five games is no doubt impressive, but Taylor has yet to rush for 100+ yards, and recent history suggests he'll do so against the Titans.
Taylor's career-high rushing yards against the Titans was just 70 yards throughout his first six matchups, but he's rushed for 100+ in his three games since, not to mention his eight total rushing touchdowns.
It won't be easy, though, given the Titans have a competent rushing defense that is T-12th best in rushing touchdowns allowed (5) and 17th in rushing yards per game allowed.
The Indianapolis Colts have one of the most expensive secondaries in the NFL.
They've rebounded, albeit marginally, since their unacceptable start, but they need to continue their upward trajectory if Indianapolis wants to leave Lucas Oil Stadium with a win.
Titans' quarterback Cam Ward has been one of the worst quarterbacks in the league through five weeks, and Colts' defensive coordinator Lou Anarumo needs to do everything in his power to not allow Ward to have a breakout performance.
Ward ranks in the following categories among qualified quarterbacks leaguewide:
179.2 passing yards per game (2nd-worst among QBs with 5 games played), 3 passing touchdowns (T-25th), 77.2 Passer Rating (28th), 5.8 % Deep Pass Rate (Last)
The Colts' secondary must take advantage of Ward's poor start to the season, especially since the defense has proven to be one of the worst tackling teams in the NFL, its revolving door at linebacker has been a glaring hindrance against the pass and run, and its pass rush cannot be trusted to take matters into its own hands.
Lou Anarumo's defense is 28th in yards allowed after contact (482) and 31st in yards per play allowed (6.8), and even though their tackling woes have been the Colts' biggest concern thus far, their pass rush (or lack thereof) has been doing its best to compete for the title of worst aspect of the defense.
Indianapolis' pass rush has totaled 10 sacks (T-19th), but the Colts' pressure rate is easily the worst (23.7%), as they are the only defense in the league with a sub-30% pressure rate, according to Next Gen Stats.
Furthermore, the Colts haven't been great against the run; in fact, they've been one of the worst, but at least they should be able to take care of the Titans' brutal run game.
Tennessee is averaging just 82.6 rushing yards per game, good for 27th-best in the NFL, and has scored the least number of touchdowns overall (6).
If Lou Anarumo's defense can't handle the Titans, the Colts' season will look even bleaker than previously thought possible.
Trusting Quenton Nelson to handle business is an easy thing to do at this point, but the future Hall of Famer will have his hands full this Sunday when he takes on a familiar foe in defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons.
Simmons is one of the highest-paid tackles in the league, and for good reason. He's become one of the best interior defensive lineman that the sport has to offers, as well as being the Titans' heart and soul of the defense.
Jeffery Simmons has 19 pressures this season, tied for the third-most among defensive tackles, including six quick pressures (under 2.5 seconds), tied for the fifth-most among defensive tackles, according to Next Gen Stats.
Since the start of the 2025 season, Simmons has 29 quick pressures, the most among defensive tackles over that span.
However, the Colts' interior O-line has allowed a 6.3% pressure rate, the 11th-lowest among teams, including just a 0.7% quick-pressure rate, trailing only the Broncos (0.6%).
Nelson and Simmons have faced off twice a season for the past several seasons, and this matchup will begin to determine just how feasible a successful season is for the Indianapolis Colts.
Noah Compton is the Publisher of Indianapolis Colts On SI. Noah is from the Indy area and has been covering the Colts since 2022, including stops at FanSided, The Blue Stable, and SBNation.

title: Colts-Titans Injury Report: Two Colts Starters Make Significant Progress
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts are preparing for a pivotal AFC South matchup against the Tennessee Titans in Week 6.
With Sunday's contest approaching, both teams are working through their final preparations while monitoring several players dealing with injuries. Thursday's practice sessions provided another update on each team's health as the Colts and Titans look to put their best lineups on the field in Nashville.
Let's take a look at the most recent injury developments for both teams.
Indianapolis Colts Injury Report (As of 10/15)
The big news of the day is Matt Goncalves and Jaylhan Tuimoloau being full participants after appearing on the injury report for concussion evaluations on Wednesday . According to James Boyd of The Athletic, neither were practicing in red non-contact jerseys, meaning they are not in concussion protocol. A significant and positive development for Sunday, as both have been evidently cleared and will be good to go this weekend barring a setback.
No practice again for Ashton Dulin. The Colts still consider him week-to-week. Jaylon Carlies missed the game in Pittsburgh and is now in danger of missing his second straight contest after not participating in either practice so far this week.
A number of veterans returned to full participation after getting the day off on Wednesday, including Keenan Allen, Jonathan Taylor and Charvarius Ward. Josh Downs, who was also listed with a hamstring injury on Wednesday, was back in full. Grover Stewart is the only new addition to the report as he gets his usual Thursday rest day.
Will Mallory continues to log full practices, a great sign of his progress working back from a thumb injury. That said, the Colts did sign tight end Pharoah Brown to their active roster from the practice squad earlier this week, bringing the number of tight ends on the roster to four. That’s likely an indication that Mallory is further behind in his rehab than the Colts are letting on.
Thursday's practice report for #TENvsIND pic.twitter.com/cAVnWjK5Lk
Two straight days of full participation for both Daniel Jones and Darius SLayton is a solid indication that both are dealing with minor knocks and are likely on track to play on Sunday. That’s great news for a passing offense that’s dealt with several issues over the first five weeks. If Slayton is healthy for the weekend, he’ll make his long awaited Indianapolis debut unless listed as a healthy scratch on game day.
Limited participation is an improvement for Jalen Travis after missing Wednesday's session. His ankle injury came up during Sunday’s loss to the Steelers, though Travis was able to return to and finish the game. We’ll know more regarding his status tomorrow, but the early indications are at least positive.
Overall, Wednesday’s report brought some worry for the Colts, but Thursday proved to be a significant step in the right direction with several starters either returning to practice or increasing their level of activity. Assuming no new developments arise between now and the final injury report, I’d expect a fairly short list on the Colts’ side of things.
Tennessee Titans Injury Report (As of 10/15)
*-On injured reserve; 21-day practice window currently open
Tennessee’s Thursday report is very similar to the first of the week. All the same names remain, but several players’ participation levels have changed.
Starting with the non-participants, Kevin Winston Jr. is yet to practice this week, indicating he may not be ready for Week 6. Tyjae Spears was limited with a knee injury on Wednesday but was downgraded to no participation on Thursday, making his availability for the weekend unlikely. As a result, the Titans’ run game will lean mostly on Tony Pollard.
Thursday’s Injury Report. pic.twitter.com/aHGH3d327n
Marcus Harris being limited is notable. Tennessee’s starting nickel has been one of the few bright spots for a floundering Titans team, recording an interception and half a sack through five games. David Martin-Robinson is the third of four tight ends listed on the depth chart, ahead of only former Colt Kylen Granson. If Martin-Robinson fails to record a full practice tomorrow, Granson could play a role against his former team.
Nothing much to note with the full participants. Tony Pollard returned from an off-day, as did John Franklin-Myers, and Cor’Dale Flott is on track to play. That said, Amani Hooker didn’t practice after being limited on Wednesday with a concussion. He’ll need to be a full participant in Friday’s practice to have any chance of clearing concussion protocol in time for the game, which seems highly unlikely at this point.
Tennessee’s secondary is the area to monitor as Week 6 approaches. With two starting cornerbacks and both starting safeties dealing with knocks, the Titans could be forced to use some backups.
Considering the wide receiver injuries on the other side for Indianapolis, that could make for a peculiar battle on game day.

title: 3 Overreactions to the Jaguars' Last-Second Loss to Texans: AFC South Shakeup
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- It is far from time for the Jacksonville Jaguars to panic, but that doesn't mean Week 6 can't be a wakeup call.
The Jaguars stormed back in the fourth quarter to give themselves a chance to win, but they failed to find a way to win the AFC South clash with the Houston Texans in London.
So, what are some overreactions to the Jaguars' 34-31 loss that are rooted in reality at 4-2? We break it down below.
Can anyone say comfortably that Brian Thomas Jr. will be ahead of Josh Cameron on the wide receiver depth chart when the Jaguars return from the bye week? Thomas had already become the forgotten man in the Jaguars' offense for the most part with just a handful of catches in the first few games, but he has caught zero passes on five targets in the last two weeks and has arguably cost the Jaguars four scoring opportunities in that span with drops. The Jaguars' staff trusts Cameron, and Jaguars quarterback Trevor Lawrence has not appeared to have any issues doing the same.
Then there is the fact that Travis Hunter got more run on offense. He didn't appear to play a heavy snap count on offense, but he did see four targets and caught them all for 59 yards and a touchdown. Had the Jaguars won, the story of the game would be Hunter's impact on offense. He will likely continue to see more touches, which really makes it seem like Thomas is receiver No. 5, and better off getting traded within the next month.
The Jaguars will be entering the bye week with a two-game lead in the AFC South since the Texans and the Indianapolis Colts are both 2-4. It is far from an awful spot to be in after the first six games, especially considering how difficult this early stretch appeared before the season began. 4-2 has long been seen as a successful outcome, and that is what the Jaguars got.
With that said, the AFC South race is now on. A two-game lead is an OK one in terms of security, but there are still 11 games to go. Things can get completely turned upside down by January if the Jaguars do not clean up their issues, because the Texans are still very much in this. Beating the Texans would have given the Jaguars a three-game cushion, a better place to be in than the one the Jaguars now occupy. The Jaguars should still feel good about the AFC South, but they could have felt great.
The Jaguars' defense had one of its worst games of the Anthony Campanile era on Sunday, allowing the Texans to score on 6-of-10 drives and allowing 34 points after allowing 40 points in the previous three games combined. C.J. Stroud picked the Jaguars apart no matter the blitz or the coverage, and the Texans also had far much more rushing success than anyone could have predicted entering the game.
"Yeah, wasn’t good enough for sure. Got to go back and look at it. Thought they made too many plays in the pass game, and they ran it better than anybody has on us so far. Got to evaluate it, get it cleaned up, but definitely disappointing," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said after the game on Sunday.
It doesn't feel fair to really throw blame at the pass-rush considering the disadvantage they were at by the field -- as evidenced by the Texans' lack of pass-rush production, which Coen noted after the game. Still, the Jaguars looked like a unit that could surely use another difference-maker on defense. They like their cornerback room, but could that be addressed with a trade before the deadline? It is worth considering after all of the big plays through the air.

title: Game Balls From Jaguars' Disheartening Loss to Texans: One Standout Emerges
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. --  The Jacksonville Jaguars will be limping into the bye week.
The Jaguars failed to get it done against the Houston Texans in Week 6, falling 34-31 on a walkoff field goal a week after their own last-second win. But even with the loss, there are still a few Jaguars who were able to move forward with strong performances and efforts. So, which of those Jaguars have earned a game ball as a result?
This one feels easy. Trevor Lawrence was one of the best players on the field on Sunday, throwing for over 300 yards and four touchdowns against a defense and a head coach that has given him fits in the past. The Texans' defense isn't what it has been in past years, but it is still a good unit with some blue-chip players on it, and Lawrence had one of the best performances of his entire career against the Texans with his latest outing.
If this is the version of Lawrence we see for the rest of the season, the Jaguars are in very good hands. He did have an end-zone interception that the Jaguars can't afford, but it did come after the Jaguars got jobbed on a bad holding call, so perhaps he never should have even been in that situation. Regardless, Lawrence had another impressive showing for the Jaguars, and once again proved to be their most important piece.
Travis Hunter was undeniably special on Sunday afternoon. Hunter gave up a few big plays, such as a long gain to Nico Collins on a stop-and-go and a few penalties, but he also made the most important play of the day for the defense. On a day where the Jaguars allowed the Texans to score on 6-of-10 drives, there were not many Jaguars defenders to consider. The Jaguars' defense got shredded, but Hunter still made an impact play with his fourth-quarter red-zone interception of C.J. Stroud.
Hunter became the first defender to intercept Stroud in 2026 with his stellar play, which ensured the Jaguars continued their run of red-zone takeaways. It was one of the only times the Jaguars slowed Houston down on Sunday, and it proved that Hunter is, at the end of the day, a play-maker who is going to get the ball. With a pass defensed against Houston, Hunter also extended his streak to five consecutive games with at least one pass defensed, tied for the longest active streak in the NFL.
"Made some critical plays for us on both sides of the football, obviously. Had the interception late, that gave us a chance to win the game. Proud of the way he completed, made some plays for us on offense and got to keep building off it," Liam Coen said after the game.
While the decision to kick the field goal by Liam Coen was certainly one that is going to be debated until the next time the Jaguars kick off, that doesn't change the fact that Cam Little was fantastic when his number was called. Little nailed the 60-yard field goal seemingly with relative ease, and it feels safe to say he could have saved the day for the Jaguars at some point if given the chance to do so.
With the kick, Little recorded the third 60-plus-yard field goal of his career, the most in franchise history. Since entering the league in 2024, his three field goals of 60-plus yards are the second most in the NFL. He is well on his way to becoming one of the highest-paid kickers in the entire NFL, because the Jaguars are tough to imagine without him and his booming field goals.
John Shipley has been covering the Jacksonville Jaguars as a beat reporter and publisher of Jaguar Report since 2019. Previously, he covered UCF's undefeated season as a beat reporter for NSM.Today, covered high school prep sports in Central Florida, and covered local sports and news for the Palatka Daily News. title: The Brian Thomas Jr. Era Effectively Ended vs. Texans, and the Jaguars' Next Steps Must Be Careful
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- For all intents and purposes, it appears the Brian Thomas Jr. era effectively ended in Week 6.
The Jaguars lost Sunday in a tight 34-31 AFC South heavyweight battle with the Houston Texans , and Thomas' performance and lack of usage and production said it all about where Thomas stands in the Jaguars' offensive plans, both today and in the future.
"Week-to-week, guys have to step up and make plays," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said bluntly after the game when asked about having confidence in Thomas moving forward after a zero-catch day that saw Thomas struggle with drops.
But that makes the Jaguars' next steps with Thomas all the more important. Here is where things could go from here, and why the Jaguars' must take a careful direction moving forward with the trade deadline a month away.
Simply put, whatever the Jaguars do with Thomas moving forward has to be considered carefully. It now looks like a mistake that the Jaguars didn't trade Thomas in the offseason, though it seems hard to believe anyone could have predicted his standing in the offense would get even worse than it was a year ago. But there is no use in crying over spille
The Jaguars' connection between Thomas and Trevor Lawrence was a big emphasis this offseason, and for good reason. According to NextGenStats, Thomas recorded 465 receiving yards on deep passes (20+ air yards) in 2024, the third-most in the NFL. But through six games, Thomas has not caught a deep pass and has been targeted on just over 10% of his deep routes. His speed is a factor to the attention it requires, but the downfield factor has completely been erased.
Thomas and Lawrence simply have not been on the same page all season. Thomas entered the week tied with Jordan Addison for No. 73 out of 74 qualified receivers in catch rate at just 50%, and that number went down on Sunday after Thomas and Lawrence failed to connect on two critical targets: an early 2nd-down throw in Texans territory that would have put the Jaguars in at least field goal range, and then an end-of-half target that could have done similar.
"Yeah, I think we just have to keep working, keep plugging away, keep finding opportunities to give him shots at the ball and I think for him, just keep playing and let the ball find you," Lawrence said. "I think that's the big thing, is don't try to chase too much and obviously we need to get him involved more and we're going to need him, so just excited for the opportunity moving forward to do that and just kind of stick with it.
"This game is funny. It doesn't always work exactly how you want it to, and sometimes things can be challenging, getting a specific guy touches and involved and just [have to] stick with it, the ball will find him. It will come his way. He's too good of a player for it not to. Just keep working, which he's done. So just keep showing up and we're going to get through it."
It has never been a work issue for Thomas, who was raved about all offseason for how much he poured into preparing for the season. It has also never been a talent issue, with Thomas flashing the high-end traits over the last two seasons that made him such a dangerous weapon. Bu it was just flashes a year ago. Now, it is hardly even that.
Thomas did not have a single 0-catch game in his career until Week 5 against the Philadelphia Eagles. He now has had two in a row, with the Jaguars throwing him five targets in the last two weeks with four incompletions and an interception. The interception was Lawrence's fault, but the other four targets were all arguably drops/failed catches by Thomas: two in the end-zone last week and two more drops this week.
Brian Thomas Jr. has to make this catch. #Jaguars #DUUUVAL pic.twitter.com/CoORZ1lEBR
There is a real chance that, coming out of the bye Thomas will be the Jaguars' fifth wide receiver like he was by the end of the game on Sunday. And he doesn't play special teams, like Josh Cameron, or defense, like Travis Hunter. So would it even be worth it to have him as active?
And that is why the Jaguars must be careful in their next steps. Once the question of being a healthy scratch has to be asked, then moves must be considered.
The trade deadline is still a month away but, as of today, the Jaguars have one of the NFL's most potentially valuable trade pieces in Thomas. He is cheap, just 23 years old, and has been a star receiver before. The former first-round pick would likely net quite the draft package, though the Jaguars have resisted the urge to deal him during the Liam Coen era.
But that likely has to change after Sunday if the Jaguars want to preserve his trade value. The Marvin Harrison Jr. trade last week should have made a potential Thomas trade open and shut when it comes to compensation, but that could change moving forward if Thomas' playing time does.
The fact that Thomas has just nine catches for 105 yards and a touchdown on 20 targets through six games is enough to already do damage to his trade value, but not enough to significantly ding it. What could ding it, though, is if the Jaguars move forward with Thomas benched.
Once the Jaguars officially bench Thomas, or even worse make him inactive, then his value truly gets tanked. The Jaguars likely feel like they need to do it for the sake of their offense considering how much his drops have hurt them, but once he isn't playing the Jaguars lose leverage in trade talks. There is no point in thinking what might have been, but getting a minor draft package for Thomas would be quite a loss considering what his value would have been this past offseason.
The Jaguars could move fast and look to trade Thomas before they kick off against the Indianapolis Colts in 14 days, which seems like the best option for both parties. Thomas' time in the sun of the Jaguars' offense seems over. It has seemed over for a while, and Sunday was simply the acceptance phase.
No matter what the Jaguars do with Thomas, they must move carefully. Trade value, and perhaps wins, depends on it.

title: 4 Winners, 7 Losers From Jaguars' Letdown vs. Texans: Welcome, Nate Boerkircher
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars won't be able to move on from this one easily.
The Jaguars had more than a few chances to make the win swing their way, but they ended up falling to the Houston Texans in a 34-31 heartbreake r in London in Week 6. So, who were the winners and stock-risers from the game, and who took steps backwards? We break it down below.
How about Nate Boerkircher? The rookie tight end caught just two passes for eight yards, but one of those was a stellar one-handed touchdown catch to help the Jaguars cut into the Texans' lead in the second-half. Boerkircher has been reliable whenever the Jaguars have thrown the ball his way, and on Sunday he showed off some of the play-making traits that made the Jaguars so interested in him with the No. 56 pick last April. The Jaguars' top pick keeps proving his worth to the Jaguars' offense, and Sunday was finally his highlight moment.
Trevor Lawrence threw four touchdowns and over 300 yards on Sunday, which you will take any week. It was the first time Lawrence has thrown 300+ yards in back-to-back weeks for the first time since 2022, and as of this writing he is the only quarterback in the NFL to throw four touchdowns in two different games. Lawrence was, once again, stellar for the Jaguars by large and large. The Jaguars were down by two scores late, but the way Lawrence played kept them in it the whole time.
Not much has to be said about this one. Hunter is the first player with a receiving touchdown and an INT in the same game since Brian Dawkins in Week 4, 2002 also vs the Texans. Hunter did not have his best game snap-to-snap, but he made some of the biggest and most important plays of the game on both sides of the ball. It feels like we are just scratching the surface of the kind of player Hunter can be and the impact he can have.
Well-done, Walker Little. The Jaguars' veteran offensive tackle had plenty of eyes on him entering the week considering the matchup with Will Anderson Jr. and Danielle Hunter, but that duo combined for one quarterback hit, zero sacks, and zero tackles for loss. Little needed to step up for the Jaguars considering Anton Harrison's injury, and Little did exactly that. Count this as a strong performance from Little.
It ... it just feels over for Brian Thomas Jr. with the Jaguars. It never felt right at the start of last year, it got worse before he became an afterthought, and then he had a stellar offseason this past summer and spring. But none of that mattered, as Thomas simply proved to be a poor fit with the Jaguars' offensive scheme by the start of the regular-season once again. Thomas was seemingly benched with zero snaps in the second-half after two costly drops that may have cost points: a drop on the first drive on second down that would have put the Jaguars in field goal range, and then a drop at the end of the half near the sideline that would have given Cam Little a chance. It just feels like it is time for both sides to move on.
I think you do have to take the field conditions into account when you look at the lack of pass-rush, because the Texans' elite pass-rush didn't register any sacks or many quarterback hits either. With that said, Hines-Allen and Walker have not gotten home very much since Week 1, and they were blanked by a bad Texans' offensive line on Sunday. The Jaguars can not have the opposing quarterback dropback 34 times and barely get touched, but that is exactly what happened to them against the Texans on Sunday.
I am a big fan of Jarrian Jones' game, and I also believe he has played better than he has been given credit for throughout the season. With that in mind, it felt like Jones had his worst game of the season on Sunday, giving up several big completions, two critical penalties, and a missed tackle on the Texans' 25-yard touchdown run. The Jaguars badly need Jones to elevate his game, which he was doing earlier in the season.
If Jones does not bounce back soon, the Jaguars might need to take a look at the trade deadline and the cornerback rooms. Montaric Brown's hamstring injury has hampered the Jaguars' cornerback depth over the last few weeks, which means the Jaguars already needed Jones to step up his game. The performance he put forth on Sunday is not what they needed to see to inspire confidence.
On one hand, I do think Anthony Campanile but a victim of his circumstances on Sunday. The defense had been stellar for five weeks and wasn't letting anyone put up points on them in doses, but the bend-don't-break defense finally broke against Houston. Part of this is because C.J. Stroud is the best quarterback the Jaguars hace faced this season, which is why I expected Stroud to have a big day. I did not expect the Jaguars to blow coverages at the rate they did on Sunday.
When that happens, there is no real place to look other than at how the defense is structured and called. Nick Caley beat Campanile in the coordinator battle this week, which is just the second time this year I think one could say that. He will need to find some answers during the bye week to keep the pass defense from sinking the Jaguars down the road.
It was the rare off game for Parker Washington, who has otherwise been stellar for the Jaguars all season long . Washington finished the game with four catches for 64 yards and he did help the Jaguars set up a scoring drive with some big catches in the first-half, but he also had 11 targets. Of those six targets to him that didn't end up in a completion, it felt like at least a few were catches he normally makes.
Washington is clearly the Jaguars' No. 1 wide receiver, and very likely will be a $30 million player sooner rather than later. But for Washington to continue to prove that he is worth that investment, he will have to come up big for them in the big games and moments like when they play their AFC South rivals ... especially the Texans.
This can't be proven in any real way, but I will say it anyways: I think the Jaguars win this game if it is played in Jacksonville. The fact the Jaguars ever had an AFC South game, let alone a game vs. the Texans, moved to London was always a travesty. Now, you see why. I said it a week ago, and I will say it again: the London games are a disadvantage. A wet, insufficient field that made it tough for anyone to get great footing instead of the sunshine and a home crowd in Florida. Are you having fun yet, London?
