title: Giants Report Card: A Winnable Game Slips Away in Week 6
full_text:
The New York Giants ’ season hit a rough patch in Week 6, marked by a lifeless running game, turnovers, penalties, and a quiet pass rush. The attack limited Cam Skattebo to six snaps and zero touches. The result was a 34-27 loss to a struggling New Orleans Saints team that got itself right against the Giants.
Some thoughts before we get to the grades…
1. People will point to Skattebo's lack of touches as a reason for the running game's dismal showing, but the run blocking also left much to be desired.
Left tackle Andrew Thomas earned the highest run-blocking grade on the offensive line, per PFF, with a 61.9. Center Bryan Hudson also earned a decent 59.8 grade, but the rest of the linemen struggled with run blocking.
2. What was receiver Malik Nabers doing on Jameis Winston’s first interception? On a play where Nabers was the intended receiver, Winston misfired the ball, and Martin Emerson Jr. picked it off, while Nabers just stood there watching instead of trying to break up the pass. The Saints converted that turnover into a 51-yard field goal to increase their lead to 27-10.
3. Per PFF, the Giants defense had 12 missed tackles in this game, two of which came on the Saints’ game-tying touchdown at the end of the first half. In the “ya think?” category, you can bet that will be a point of emphasis in the coming week of practice.
4. Despite the loss — and this one falls into the category of a game that the Giants had no business losing — New York is still in first place in the NFC East. But it won’t stay there if it doesn’t clean things up fast. The Giants have a much tougher second half of the schedule after their bye week.
5. Since no one among the running backs took the bull by the horns, does it make sense for the Giants to look to trade for a running back before the deadline? Given the lack of patience Harbaugh showed this week, would anyone be surprised if that happened?
Head coach John Harbaugh said running back Cam Skattebo’s lack of touches in this game wasn’t by design , even though Najee Harris saw more snaps this week on offense.
Circumstances aside, the Giants offense is going nowhere with this running game. The unit finished with an average of 4.2 yards per carry, but a 28-yard run by quarterback J.J. McCarthy and a 20-yard reverse by receiver Darnell Mooney inflated that figure. Strip the rushing yardage down to just Harris, Tyrone Tracy Jr., and Devin Singletary, and the average falls to 2.4 yards per carry.
And no, Jameis Winston did not play well either, and chances are he’s lost his starting job moving forward. Unless the Giants solve their running game issues fast, expect more struggles to win and win big from this offense.
Twelve missed tackles, 4.6 yards per carry allowed in the run game, zero sacks. A glaring miscommunication on the Saints’ second-quarter touchdown. A needless roughing-the-passer penalty against outside linebacker Kayvon Thibodeaux. Need we say any more?
Charlie Jones had an absolute killer turnover on a kickoff return that the Saints cashed in for a score and a major momentum swing. The Saints got the better of the Giants’ coverage units, averaging 28.3 yards on kickoff returns and 13.6 yards on punt returns, with several big gains.
Dominic Zvada bounced back from last week’s shaky day, and Jordan Stout was his usual reliable self. Still, the Giants lost the field-position battle this week, which didn’t help.
John Harbaugh said he’s looking for someone to take the bull by the horns at running back, yet he won’t let anyone even try to get into a rhythm, which perplexed Najee Harris, among others, in the postgame locker room.
Harbaugh can say all he wants that Skattebo’s lack of touches wasn’t a benching. Semantically, he’s correct, but it was clearly an attempt to send a message to the young running back that he needs to be better.
That said, is this how it’s going to be when someone makes a mistake moving forward? Accoutnability is one thing, but at what point does there need to be an attempt to work harder to correct a problem rather tan try to sweep it under the rug?

title: McCarthy Makes History in Relief, but Giants Fall Short vs. Saints
full_text:
EAST RUTHERFORD, NJ — New York Giants quarterback J.J. McCarthy did not set out to make history during the team’s Week 6 showdown with the New Orleans Saints.
Yet, with just over 11 minutes left in the fourth quarter and New Orleans holding a 34-10 lead, the Michigan product stepped onto the field to relieve beleaguered starter Jameis Winston.
McCarthy orchestrated three late-game scoring drives and helped the Giants nearly complete an improbable comeback in the eventual 34-27 loss at MetLife Stadium.
His 243 passing yards in the fourth quarter were the most by any player in 11 minutes of play in NFL history.
For McCarthy, however, giving his team a chance to earn the win was all that mattered.
“I believe it was like 10 or 12 minutes left in the fourth quarter, but my mentality stays the same every time I step on the field,” McCarthy said. “Do my job in those six seconds, and do it to the best of my ability, and do anything I can to help the team move the ball.”
Despite his record-setting day, McCarthy left the field with mixed emotions. Though he remained proud of his performance, the 10th overall selection in the 2024 NFL Draft fell short of his ultimate goal,: to bring the Giants a win.
On New York’s final drive, McCarthy ran for 28 yards and completed 20-yard and 9-yard passes to tight end Isaiah Likely and receiver Malik Nabers, respectively. Unfortunately, the drive was littered with four incompletions — the last of which resulted in a turnover on downs on 4th-and-1 deep in New Orleans’ red zone.
In that regard, McCarthy will use the game’s ending sequence to motivate improvement heading into Week 7 and beyond.
“I’m not pleased when we lose,” McCarthy said. “At the end of the day, no matter what happens, we try to get that 1-0 win every week, and I’ve got to look back at the tape and find ways to get better.”
Still, the 23-year-old has reason to be confident in his performance. He finished the game having completed 11-of-21 passes for the aforementioned 243 yards and one touchdown. Per ESPN, McCarthy had the most passing yards in a fourth quarter by any player this season, and the second-most passing yards in a fourth quarter by any quarterback who didn’t start over the last 25 seasons.
He also rushed twice for 26 net yards, allowing coordinator Matt Nagy to keep his run-centric, motion-based offense. Though he may be the talk of the Tri-State area for the next few days, McCarthy was content to credit his teammates for helping him feel right at home.
“I was just really proud of the guys around me, just responding and always keeping that belief that we can win this thing,” McCarthy said. “That’s going to be huge going down the stretch, and I’m just really proud of the guys around me.”
“I felt like I was protected every single play I was in there,” he added. “The offensive line played great, receivers caught the balls, running backs did their thing when they needed to, and it was just a really awesome group to be a part of.”
Since the Giants sent a 2027 fifth-round draft pick to the Minnesota Vikings in exchange for his services in late September, McCarthy has impressed his coaches and teammates with his strong work ethic and quick ability to understand and apply what he’s learned.
As a result, he quickly worked his way from Big Blue’s third stringer to their top backup, who could also be used in a package of gadget run-plays. In Week 6, he got the chance to run the Giants’ offense — and he made the most of it.
With New York’s Week 7 matchup against the Houston Texans looming, questions about his future role will only intensify. However, McCarthy is happy to be a part of a team that refuses to quit — even in the face of adversity.
“Yeah, I’m extremely impressed,” McCarthy said of his team’s determination. “This team, since I got in the door, you could tell there was something special about them. The way Coach Harbaugh instills this kind of confidence and belief is through the work and the preparation, and it’s not just talk.
“Just being able to be a part of this group is extremely special,” he continued. “They were going to keep having to build that resilience along the way. Earlier in the year, with (Brian) Burns and Jax (Jaxson Dart) going down, that’s huge. But seeing how they responded, it’s a really special group.”

title: Cam Skattebo's Lack of Touches Wasn't By Design, Claims John Harbaugh
full_text:
New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh denied that the coaches had decided to bench running back Cam Skattebo, who has had a bit of a fumbling problem of late, in the team’s 34-27 Week 6 loss to the New Orleans Saints.
But they might as well have benched him, considering Skattebo didn’t get a single touch, either as a rusher or receiver, in the game.
“It was not by design. All those guys were taking equal reps in the first half. We were trying to see who could make something happen, who could get a hot hand and earn it. Nobody has really taken the bull by the horns,” Harbaugh insisted.
“So, we put four guys up and see if we can get something going with the running game. That was the idea. They were all pretty equal, I think, in the first half.”
But that wasn’t quite the case. Skattebo, one of those four, didn’t see a single ball come his way, and he was limited to six snaps on offense.
“You’re balancing between four guys. Do the math. How many plays were there? And that was our plan. Now you can argue that. You can say, well, I don’t like that. I don’t like you divvying up the snaps between four backs. And I can tell you, I don’t like it either. One of those guys needs to step up.
“Somebody needs to step up and be the back. And none of those guys have done that yet. And when one of those guys steps up to be the back, then they’ll be the back. That’s your answer. And that’s as honest as I can be about it.”
Skattebo took the high road of accountability.
“I got punished for what I did, and I understand,” he said, referring to his fumbling issue, which last week cost the Giants a chance to win their game against Washington. “So I got to be ready when coach calls my name, and that wasn’t today.”
While Skattebo knew his reps would be reduced, he didn’t know by how much.
“I didn’t expect to have zero (carries),” he said. “I was expecting not to play as much, just like I did. And the message was, you know, keep your head down; I gotta keep going, you know. They understand the type of player I am, and I gotta continue to do my job and do it to the best of my ability.”
Skattebo admitted that being involved in the offense was hard, but he reiterated that he understood where the coaches were coming from.
“I’ve made mistakes, and I gotta own up to them,” he said. “And if that is what they wanna do is keep me on the sidelines because of that, I totally understand. You know, I can’t make mistakes at this level of this game. And when you make mistakes like that, there are consequences to be made.”

title: Giants Fall Short vs. Saints, and the McCarthy-Winston Debate Is On
full_text:
EAST RUTHERFORD, NJ — It was only a matter of time before questions about J.J. McCarthy supplanting Jameis Winston as the New York Giants’ starting quarterback began in earnest.
That time has come after the Giants dropped a disappointing 34-27 loss to the New Orleans Saints. They seemed to get new life when McCarthy, who up until that point had only been inserted into the game for a single RPO in the first half, took over for starter Jameis Winston in the fourth quarter.
He led the team on drives that resulted in 17 unanswered points, but the comeback fell short by a touchdown with less than a minute to go in regulation.
McCarthy finished 11-of-21 for 243 yards, averaging 11.6 yards per attempt. He took one sack and threw one touchdown and one interception. More importantly, he showed his mobility, finishing as the Giants’ leading rusher with 26 yards on two carries as he tried to rally Big Blue from behind.
To be fair to Winston, the sluggish offensive showing was not all his fault. The Giants had absolutely no running game against a Saints run defense that entered this week ranked 30th in the league.
Cam Skattebo, the team’s RB1, has had ball-security issues the last three weeks and got no rushing attempts or pass targets.
The Giants’ other three running backs (Tyrone Tracy Jr., Najee Harris and Devin Singletary) failed to step up and take the bull by the horns.
They combined to rush for 34 yards on 14 carries, a 2.43-yard-per-carry average, not much of an improvement after compiling a dismal nine yards on eight carries in the first half.
The Giants also weren’t helped by their special teams units, particularly on coverage. The Saints averaged 13.6 yards per punt return and 28.3 yards per kickoff return, while the Giants averaged 8.3 yards and 22.4 yards on punt and kickoff returns.
The unit also had a backbreaking fumble on a kickoff return that the Saints not only recovered but also converted into a 5-play scoring drive, resulting in a 2-yard touchdown pass from Saints quarterback Tyler Shough to receiver Bryce Lance to make it a 10-10 game.
And the defense was no better, missing 11 tackles according to PFF, while the run defense had another poor showing, allowing the Saints to average 4.6 yards per carry (38 carries, 175 yards and one touchdown).
“I thought he came in there and did a heck of a job given the circumstances, you know, and kind of desperation time,” head coach John Harbaugh said of McCarthy.
“It’s different from normal football, but we made some plays and got us back, gave us a chance to win the game, and we’re throwing the ball in the endzone at the end, so that was good. You’ve got to compliment him on that.”
All that said, where the Giants go from here likely boils down to what they do at quarterback. And it’s hard to deny that Winston left a lot of plays on the field while McCarthy, who tied a Giants single-game record with his 243 passing yards in the fourth quarter (the mark last set by Eli Manning back in 2012), took advantage of whatever snaps he received during garbage time.
Harbaugh wasn’t ready to make any snap decisions on which quarterback will get the start next week against Houston.
“It’s not even up for discussion or conversation right now,” he said, somewhat annoyed by the question. “We’ve got to go back and go to work.
“I have no problem with Jameis whatsoever. I love the way he competes, I love the way he fights, all those kinds of things. He was up and down today for sure, but those things will all be decided not ten minutes after a game.”
Still, it’s going to be hard to ignore what McCarthy brought to the table, even if it came in garbage time, because he made the game far more competitive.

title: Giants Week 6 Injury Round Up: Newsome, Thomas and Mooney Exit Team's 34-27 Loss to Saints Early
full_text:
EAST RUTHERFORD, NJ — Very little went right for the New York Giants during much of the second half of their Week 6 matchup against the New Orleans Saints.
Playing at home at MetLife in near-perfect weather, the Giants watched a 10-3 second-half lead deteriorate as the visiting Saints took a commanding lead into the fourth quarter. Despite New York’s best late-game efforts, they ultimately fell short in a 34-27 loss to the Saints.
Unfortunately for the Giants, they also monitored the health of three key players for the rest of the contest.
Giants cornerback Greg Newsome II left the game in the third quarter to be evaluated for a concussion. He was ultimately ruled out for the remainder of the game.
With approximately seven minutes remaining in the fourth quarter, the Giants also lost offensive lineman Andrew Thomas for concussion evaluation. Thomas had been questionable heading into Week 6 due to a groin injury, but was active for the start of the game.
Thomas cleared the evaluation, which was called for by the spotter after he struggled to get up off the ground due to his groin injury. At that point, Thomas said that the coach decided to keep him out of the game and roll with rookie J.C. Davis at left tackle.
Lastly, receiver Darnell Mooney left the game in the third quarter to be evaluated for a neck injury. His return was listed as questionable.
Thomas, New York’s starting left tackle, has been a key component through the first five games of the season. The 6-foot-5, 315-pounder entered this game having allowed 11 total pressures in pass protection — including one sack and three hits allowed to opposing pass rushers, per PFF.
Newsome is the Giants’ starting cornerback on the right side of the perimeter. The veteran defensive back entered the game having compiled 22 total tackles and one interception on the season. Newsome II broke up three passes in coverage and allowed a 64.4 passer rating when targeted by opposing quarterbacks.
Mooney entered the game with eight catches on 17 targets for 109 receiving yards and 0 touchdowns. He averaged 13.6 yards per reception on the season. The 28-year-old scored an impressive 20-yard run on the Giants’ first scoring drive of the day.
The Giants entered Week 6 with their share of injuries. Three of their inactive players — Theo Johnson (neck), safety Tyler Nubin (neck) and cornerback Colton Hood (concussion) — were listed as out on the week’s final injury report.
Right tackle Jermaine Eluemunor (calf), who was also listed as questionable, was ultimately declared inactive after team staff evaluated him during pregame warmups to test his injured leg. Swing tackle Marcus Mbow replaced him.
Safety Jason Pinnock returned from a concussion he suffered in Week 4. Pinnock got the start next to veteran Jevon Holland, giving the injured Nubin a rest.
Outside linebacker Abdul Carter (calf) was also active, despite having been listed as questionable on Friday’s report.

title: Giants Comeback Bid Falls Short in 34-27 Loss to Saints
full_text:
EAST RUTHERFORD, NJ — The New York Giants nearly pulled off a comeback in their Week 6 matchup with the New Orleans Saints.
Amid pleasant autumn weather at MetLife Stadium, the Giants nearly erased a 24-point fourth-quarter deficit — after surrendering a 10-point lead in the first half — in an eventual 34-27 loss to the Saints.
Starting quarterback Jameis Winston completed 14 of 26 passes for 152 yards with one touchdown. However, two costly Winston interceptions led coach John Harbaugh to install backup J.J. McCarthy for much of the second half.
The 10th overall pick in the 2024 NFL Draft went 11-of-21 for 243 yards, one touchdown, and one interception — ultimately orchestrating three fourth-quarter scoring drives. Yet the Giants couldn't convert on 4th-and-1 at the Saints’ 14-yard line with time expiring.
With the loss, the Giants drop to 3-2-1through six games in the 2026 NFL season.
The Giants struck first in Week 6 by compiling a 12-play, 93-yard scoring drive on their second possession. Receiver Darnell Mooney showcased his rushing skills by ripping a 20-yard run on 1st-and-10 from New York’s own 23.
Winston connected with tight end Isaiah Likely twice for 11 and 24 yards, respectively, advancing the Giants deep into Saints’ territory.
Facing 3rd-and-6 at New Orleans’ 17, New York’s veteran quarterback beat the defensive pressure to find running back Tyrone Tracy, Jr. for the 17-yard catch-and-run, giving Big Blue an early 7-0 lead on the leaping touchdown.
TRACE LEAPS IN FOR SIX 🫡 📺: FOX pic.twitter.com/46WyC4t2iK
New York’s second scoring series took 4:27 off the clock in the second quarter. Winston led the Giants on a 10-play, 39-yard drive, highlighted by a 19-yard pass to receiver Malik Nabers to put the Giants into the Saints’ side of the field.
Despite taking what would have been a six-yard loss on a sack from New Orleans defender Vernon Broughton — who easily bypassed Giants guard Sisi Mauigoa — the hit was ruled a head-to-head penalty, which advanced New York 15 yards into the red zone. Rookie kicker Dominic Zvada connected on a 34-yard field goal, extending the Giants' lead to 10-0.
New Orleans, however, refused to be held scoreless in the first half. In just 1:09, quarterback Tyler Shough used six plays to advance his team 16 yards, 12 of which came on a pass over the middle to receiver Chris Olave. Saints kicker Daniel Carlson made a 58-yard field goal to put his team up 10-3.
In a reversal of fortune, Giants returner Charlie Jones fumbled the ensuing kickoff, allowing Saints tight end Oscar Delp to recover at New York’s 28-yard line.
Shough scrambled for 25 yards to the Giants’ 3-yard line before he threw a two-yard touchdown pass to receiver Bryce Lance. Carlson’s extra point tied the game at 10 to close the first half.
The Saints marched into the second half, determined to build on the momentum they gained from their late second-quarter surge.
On their opening drive in the third quarter, Shough led his team on a 5-play, 79-yard scoring drive. While the series was highlighted by a 17-yard run from Saints running back CJ Donaldson, it was also defined by a 15-yard roughing-the-passer penalty on defender Kayvon Thibodeaux.
Star back Alvin Kamara provided the crescendo, taking Shough’s short pass for a 31-yard score. Carlson’s extra point gave the Saints their first lead of the day at 17-10.
New York’s regression continued on the Saints’ next offensive possession. After the Giants were forced to punt, New Orleans traveled 52 yards on nine plays, highlighted by a 10-yard completion to Olave to put the visitors at the doorstep of the red zone. Shough took the ball into the end zone himself on the one-yard QB sneak, giving his club a 24-10 lead.
New Orleans ended the third quarter by adding three more points to their lead with a six-play, 30-yard series.
After cornerback Martin Emerson, Jr. intercepted Winston in Saints territory, running backs Kendre Miller and Kamara helped put the team in position for Carlson to attempt a 51-yard field goal. New Orleans began to pull away, taking a 27-10 advantage.
After New York’s defense forced a three-and-out on New Orleans’ first possession in the fourth quarter, Winston threw his second costly interception of the day—a deep attempt to find Likely that Saints safety Julian Blackmon snagged.
Taking over at the Giants' 21-yard line, Shough needed only two plays to find Olave for the 18-yard touchdown pass, giving New Orleans a commanding 34-10 lead.
Still, the home team had some fight remaining.
With Winston yielding the ball to McCarthy, the Giants engineered three straight scoring drives. The Michigan product’s first scoring series saw New York advance 52 yards on six plays, culminating in a 5-yard touchdown run from Tyrone Tracy. The Saints cut the lead to 34-18 after a successful two-point conversion.
McCarthy once again orchestrated some late-game magic, taking the Giants 73 yards on just three plays. He tossed his first touchdown as a Giant — a 24-yard strike to Isaiah Likely.
Despite the failed two-point conversion, the Giants climbed back into the game at 34-24.
J.J. finds Isaiah Likely 🙌 📺: FOX pic.twitter.com/0fLSL9TMTV
New York appeared determined to complete the comeback, as McCarthy led a seven-play, 69-yard drive which was capped by a successful 41-yard field goal attempt. With just over two minutes remaining, the Giants had sliced New Orleans’ lead to 34-27.
Unfortunately, Big Blue couldn't put any additional points on the board. Despite starting their final possession with a 28-yard run from McCarthy, the quarterback’s fourth-down pass to Likely was incomplete. The Giants ultimately turned the ball over on downs, allowing New Orleans to take one snap in victory formation.
FINAL: New Orleans 34, New York 27

In addition to “Crucial Catch” campaign signage adorning MetLife Stadium, Winston personally hosted 10 breast cancer survivors in observance of October’s Breast Cancer Awareness Month.

title: Giants-Saints Live Blog: Big Blue Looks to Stack Wins at MetLife
full_text:
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. – The New York Giants return home Sunday to face the New Orleans Saints with a simple goal: stack wins.
That’s been the message since the start of the season for the Giants, who lead the NFC East by 1.5 games. Undefeated at home, they are looking to add another win to that record as they continue striving to match their 6-0 start at home achieved in 2008.
They will face a battered and bruised Saints team that has won the last three meetings but hasn’t had its luck this season. New Orleans is trying to snap a three-game losing streak and make up ground in a winnable NFC South, but numerous issues from personnel to coaching have caused the Saints to sputter.
Here are some storylines that will play out as the game unfolds.
The Saints have the league’s 30th-ranked run defense, allowing 4.9 yards per carry. The Giants’ ground game has averaged just 3.7 yards per attempt since Jaxson Dart’s season-ending knee injury.
Will the Giants’ ground game snap out of its funk? Moreover, will the running back carries be redistributed given lead running back Cam Skattebo’s recent ball-security issues?
The Giants have recorded seven sacks over the last two weeks thanks in part to a heavier reliance on the blitz. The Saints’ offensive line, meanwhile, has allowed three sacks against quarterback Tyler Shough in that span.
Per Next Gen Stats, Giants cornerback Deonte Banks has been targeted 22 times this season and has allowed 11 receptions for 99 yards. His 50% completion rate allowed is tied for the fifth-lowest among all players targeted at least 20 times, and second-lowest among NFC players.
It’s unknown whether defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson plans to have his cornerbacks travel with specific receivers. Still, the possibility of Banks covering Chris Olave, the Saints’ top wideout, is intriguing, and the result could significantly affect the outcome.
The Giants and Saints kick off at 1:05 p.m. at MetLife Stadium. Follow along with our interactive blog, featuring game highlights, scoring plays, stats, injury updates, and more.

title: Why the Giants Will Beat the Saints, Why They Won’t, and a Prediction
full_text:
The New York Giants host a struggling New Orleans Saints team looking to snap a three-game losing streak that has drawn attention and stern words from team owner Gayle Benson this past week.
The Saints have the league’s 20th-ranked offense (322.0 yards per game) and the 25th-ranked defense (361.0 yards per game) as they head into MetLife Stadium against a Giants team that has a chance to go 4-0 at home for the first time since 2008, when they got off to a 6-0 start at home.
Despite the Saints’ struggles, they enter this game as a 1.5-point favorite per FanDuel , which is a head-scratcher considering they have averaged 21.3 points in their last three games, while the home team has averaged 25 points per game.
But odds aside, the NFC East-leading Giants’ goal, according to head coach John Harbaugh, is simple: stack wins.
“You always know what they are, but you know you’ve got to stack wins to make the December standings matter,” Harbaugh said when asked how much he pays attention to the standings at this point in the season. “So, we focus on the next game.”
The Giants, according to Tankathon , have to make hay, so to speak. They face a remaining schedule with a combined winning percentage of .484, with their four toughest opponents being the 49ers, Jaguars, Lions, and Browns.
All four of those challenging opponents land on the schedule after the Giants’ Week 8 bye.
But to focus on what the Giants might do this week, let’s look at the best- and worst-case scenarios.
If there was ever a good week for the Giants’ rushing game to snap out of its funk, this would be it. The league’s 30th-ranked run defense has struggled big time this season, allowing 4.9 yards per rushing attempt.
It also ranks last in the league in defensive rush success (52.5%), meaning it struggles to stop opponents from gaining the minimum required yardage on a run (excluding kneeldowns and scrambles).
The Giants’ rushing offense has not been the same since quarterback Jaxson Dart landed on IR with a season-ending knee injury. Although it ranks 17th in total rushing yards, it also averages a dismal 3.7 yards per attempt, 24th in the league.
As if the rushing game’s struggles aren’t enough, it will be interesting to see if Harbaugh decides to reduce running back Cam Skattebo’s touches this week given his fumbling issue.
As usual, the head coach was mum on the plans, but this could be a week when Najee Harris and Tyrone Tracy Jr. get bigger roles in the rushing attack to see if they can jumpstart it.
On the defensive side, the Giants’ pass rush has finally awakened after a slow start, recording seven sacks over the last two weeks. This week, they face a Saints offensive line that has surrendered three sacks to quarterback Tyler Shough over that same period.
Combine that with the opportunistic Giants secondary, which has forced eight turnovers this season , against a Saints offense that has committed 13 giveaways, and the Giants’ quest to remain undefeated at home could get a lot easier.
The Giants’ run defense, in Harbaugh’s words, has been “feast or famine” this season. Last week in the tie against Washington, it was clearly the latter, having surrendered a season-high 202 yards on the ground.
There are many reasons for the Giants’ struggles in run defense, but one glaring issue has been facing pre-snap motion.
Motion changes the look for the defense and has sometimes left players out of position or forced them into bad angles as they try to stop the play from gaining a lot of yards.
Under head coach Kellen Moore, the Saints have deployed pre-snap motion on 64% of their offensive snaps this season, the ninth-highest rate in the league, and have a 46% success rate overall when using motion. While they use pre-snap motion more in the passing game, they have used it at a 35% rate in the rushing game.
If the Giants, who have allowed opponents 5.2 yards per rush attempt on first down, can’t tighten that up, the Saints will have options on subsequent downs, giving New Orleans an advantage.
The other thing that could spoil the Giants’ quest to win their fourth straight game at home is their own aggressiveness on defense.
If the Giants, who over the last two weeks have blitzed on 57.8% of opposing quarterbacks’ drop backs, come at the Saints with a similar rate of pressure, they’d better hope that Saints signal-caller Tyler Shough, who per PFF data, has a 102.7 passer rating when throwing the ball in 2.5 seconds or less, doesn’t connect with receivers Chris Olave and Rashid Shaheed for the big pass plays downfield.
If I live to be 100 (fingers crossed), I will never understand how the oddsmakers come up with their weekly point spreads.
What I do understand is that Harbaugh has this team dialed in, and this matchup against the Saints is overall favorable for the Giants if they play a relatively clean game and keep the ball-security issues out of the mix.
The Giants have a lot more going for them at this point in the season than the Saints, including far too many advantages that, if they hit on all cylinders, will get the job done.

title: 4 Studs & 4 Duds in Jets' Week 6 Loss to Patriots: Aaron Glenn fumbles, David Bailey Shines
full_text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — Not all losses are created equal. But for a team looking to improve on the scoreboard, even a hard-fought loss to a division rival isn't good enough for the New York Jets and head coach Aaron Glenn.
Gang Green battled hard, but similar mental and physical mistakes cost them dearly in a 26-19 loss to the New England Patriots on Sunday.
"I don't think anybody feels good about being 2-4, but I do feel good about the effort that we played with," Jets head coach Aaron Glenn said. "I do feel good about a number of things that we're doing. There are just some things that we have to get ready to fix."
It appeared New England was going to run away with the game after one half of play. They led 17-3 and took advantage of several coaching mishaps by the Jets. But New York clawed its way back in the third quarter to cut the deficit to four going into the final frame.
From there, though, New York failed to take advantage of opportunities and ended up losing to a Patriots offense that saw three touchdown passes by Drake Maye. The loss drops them to 2-4 on the year.
Despite the loss, there were still plenty of studs from the Jets, and a fair share of duds. Let's go through the list now.
The best overall player on the day for New York was Braelon Allen and it wasn't close. New York's power back repeatedly ran Patriots players over and kept the Jets offense on schedule for most of the afternoon.
In total, Allen recorded 78 yards rushing on 17 carries and added 26 yards receiving on two catches. That comes out to 19 touches, 104 scrimmage yards, and 5.4 yards per touch.
And the coaching staff was thrilled.
"Braelon was doing a hell of a job, and he was popping those runs," Glenn said.
The more Allen plays like this, the more obvious it is that the team needs to split his carries with Breece Hall when he comes back from injury - not keeping him just a situational back.
New York's coaching staff may have been pleased with their running game, but it's clear how much of a hindrance they were for the entire roster on Sunday. Any football game can be chalked down to coaching and players executing.
The problem is the Jets executed. New York's coaches didn't put them in good positions to succeed, though.
Here was my tally on some of Glenn's biggest mistakes from the afternoon.
And that was all in the first half. All in all, the coaching staff does get credit for making adjustments to start the second half. New York never quit, and the fact that they had the Patriots battling late in the fourth is a good step.
But it wasn't just Glenn who struggled. Offensive coordinator Frank Reich has watched his starting offense get players healthy, and be unable to do anything with the new pieces. New York has failed to put up more than 20 points in each of their last three games. He also has struggled to find answers when teams send pressure.
2-4 is 2-4. Aaron Glenn is 5-18 as a head coach. Frank Reich's offense is among the worst in the league. Until those numbers change, there will be concern if New York has the right man in charge.
What a debut for Omar Cooper Jr. The rookie out of Indiana missed the last four weeks due to an ankle injury suffered on opening day. In his first full game as a member of the Jets, the 30th overall pick caught six passes for 103 yards and his first career touchdown.
"I feel great. I was grateful that God blessed me a lot to have that opportunity," Cooper said. "It was a great feeling, felt good to finally be able to be back out there."
Cooper is the second Jets rookie to record 100 yards receiving after Kenyon Sadiq recorded one in a Week 3 loss to the Detroit Lions. If Cooper can build off this performance, it should make New York's offense an explosive group moving forward.
This was an encouraging breakout for the rookie receiver after missing so much time.
Not a lot went right for the Jets defense on Sunday, especially within the line of scrimmage. One player who did perform well, though, was linebacker Jamien Sherwood. The veteran linebacker has struggled to start the season but was one of the Jets' better defensive players on Sunday.
He led the team with 11 tackles, one for a loss. He also added a fumble recovery and a quarterback hit.
His best play came late in the game. Maye found Demario Douglas for a deep completion, one that seemed to be a sure-fire touchdown. But Sherwood chased after the receiver and ended up forcing a fumble on the play. Sherwood never gave up on the play. That's something Glenn and the rest of the defense will appreciate.
After a slow start, Sherwood is starting to play pretty well. On Sunday, he might have had his best game in years.
New York's coaching staff was horrible all game. One group who was just as bad if not worse was their interior line.
The Jets needed to control the line of scrimmage on both sides of the ball if they had any hope of pulling off an upset. Offensively, the team gave up three sacks, struggled against pressure, and failed on multiple short-yardage situations. Defensively, the Patriots bracketed Will McDonald and David Bailey and dared their interior defensive linemen to make a play.
The collective of Jowon Briggs, Harrison Phillips, and T'Vondre Sweat was nonexistent when it came to generating pressure. Just as they have been all season.
"It's hard to explain, to be honest with you, because I have all the confidence in the world in our front and being able to cause havoc," Glenn said. "I give them credit, they did a good job of chipping and thumping and doing all they can to our edge guys, and that was their deal. We've got to do a better job of now getting some of this interior pressure."
This group needs to play a lot better moving forward.
New York's defensive line was a disaster all game. They were blown off the ball, and got minimal pressures all game. In fact, second-overall pick David Bailey put up a goose egg in sacks after a three-sack day the week prior.
Still, Bailey found a way to be impactful. The edge rusher forced a fumble midway through the third quarter deep in Patriots territory. He has improved in run defense, and while he wasn't as dominant compared to past weeks, the fact Bailey's bad game still saw a big play made is a really good thing for the Jets.
Especially since the Patriots made it a goal to make sure he wouldn't beat them all game.
A.J. Brown spent the better part of the last two seasons crying about his desire to be one of the greatest receivers of all time and needing an elite quarterback to do so. Turns out, even having an elite quarterback didn't exactly help him on Sunday.
Brown dropped four passes and was easily New England's worst offensive player on the field. He's missed the last few weeks with an ankle injury so rust could have played a part in his poor performance.
But from not celebrating with the team when they scored a touchdown, to so many dropped passes, it might have been one of the worst games of Brown's career.
Make no mistake, the Jets may have a major problem on their hands when it comes to Garrett Wilson. The star receiver has been a consummate professional throughout the four losing seasons he's been with the team. Even to begin this year, he has been relatively patient as the new offense gets installed.
Sunday's performance showed just how frustrated the receiver is. And it's not his fault either.
Wilson saw just six targets on the day and just two going into the fourth quarter. While he finished with four receptions and was followed by Patriots star cornerback Christian Gonzalez, New York did very little to get the ball into his hands.
"I try and reason it in my head because we've got a whole other fourth quarter and I know that the game can change at any moment," Wilson said after the game. "Just try and keep playing my role, waiting for that moment that they want to call on me."
And that's a reflection of offensive coordinator Frank Reich's poor ability to scheme players open for success. Unless things change, it may not…

title: Frank Reich Is Among 3 Jets to Blame for Sunday's 26-19 Loss to the Patriots
full_text:
Any goodwill that the Jets created with last week's win over the Browns was erased on Sunday afternoon. Entering Week 6 one win away from the .500 mark, the Jets are back to being two games below a winning record after a 26-19 loss to the Patriots, which was more out of reach than the final score suggests.
New York fell behind New England towards the end of the first quarter and could never retake the lead after Jason Sanders opened the scoring with a 42-yard field goal. From then on, the Jets couldn't get key stops when they needed them, nor could they convert when it mattered most.
Now, they're about to enter Week 7 with a 2-4 record, making a potential playoff push an uphill battle.
As head coach Aaron Glenn starts to figure out how to get his team back on track, here's a look at the three Jets who deserve most of the blame for Sunday afternoon's defeat.
A new week, but the same old story for Frank Reich's offense .
The Jets' offensive coordinator, once again, struggled to keep his unit on the field throughout the game. Sure, they controlled the ball (30:03) slightly more than the Patriots (29:57), but that doesn't mean much when New York's offense is going 3-for-10 on third downs (30%), while New England went 8-for-15 (53.3%) in that regard.
Reich's play-calling was egregious, especially when the Jets handed the ball to Isaiah Williams on third-and-one in the first half—a move that failed—despite the fact that Braelon Allen had racked up 30-plus yards on that drive. Additionally, New York went 0-for-2 on fourth downs and 0-for-3 on red-zone scoring attempts.
Reich was supposed to be the key to unlocking the Jets' offense, but that clearly hasn't been the case. If Gang Green can't put points on the board against the lowly Dolphins next week, it's fair to wonder if it's time for New York to hire a new offensive coordinator.
Isaiah Davis's lack of usage was one of the bigger head-scratchers early in the Jets' campaign. Despite averaging 5.6 yards on 73 carries in the 2024 and 2025 seasons, New York didn't give Davis any offensive snaps until Week 3 vs. Detroit, with his first carries not coming until he turned a pair into eight yards against Cleveland last week.
Although he saw more action against the Patriots, Davis didn't exactly make the most of his eight touches (seven carries, one catch). Plays often died in his hands, as he recorded 16 rushing yards for an average of 2.3 yards per attempt, including multiple third- and fourth-and-one stops. His longest run of the day was nine yards, which means he averaged 1.2 yards on the other six.
Instead of showing his coaches why he should be on the field, Davis gave the Jets more reasons to use him less on offense and more on special teams moving forward. There's no telling if or when he'll get another chance to prove his worth, especially with Breece Hall's return eventually coming.
It isn't a secret that Dane Belton has been one of the Jets' best offseason additions . He's a big reason why New York's secondary has improved this season, but that doesn't mean he's incapable of making his own fair share of mistakes.
After all, Belton seemed to be the one who was supposed to cover tight end Hunter Henry on the seven-yard touchdown (h/t NFL) that gave the Patriots a 10-point fourth-quarter lead. In the embedded video, linebacker Demario Douglas can be seen turning to Belton with confusion, further suggesting that a communication breakdown was at play.
Hunter Henry is wide open and extends the @Patriots lead! NYJvsNE on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/XLoJlTgMzs
While Belton finished with nine tackles and a defended pass, his 54.7 Pro Football Focus grade is his second-worst mark of the season, trailing only Week 2 (52.4). He graded well against the run (87.7) but was also given a poor mark for coverage (45.8), which was the third-worst on the team this weekend.
Hopefully, it's only a one-off dud for Belton, who's proven that he can be a difference-maker this season. It just happens that the difference he made on Sunday wasn't the good kind, leaving it to time to tell whether he can bounce back against the Dolphins at MetLife Stadium next week.

title: On SI Exclusive: Will McDonald IV Still Has Big Goals for Jets' Pass Rush Despite Slow Start
full_text:
FLORHAM PARK, N.J. — Even when he was drafted by the Jets in 2023, it felt like Will McDonald IV  was someone New York fans wouldn't truly get behind .
First, it was the fact that the team seemed to take another edge rusher despite already having a plethora of them. Many wanted Broderick Jones, but that became impossible when the Steelers and Patriots worked on a trade to spurn the Jets.
Then, as Jaxon Smith-Njigba became an All-Pro, frustration shifted to the Jets choosing McDonald over him. Through all the anger, McDonald has not wavered. He understands his importance to Gang Green and has a desire to continue to play the game at a high level.
"I'm just trying to improve and make plays," McDonald told Sports Illustrated . "Our D-line is working together, but we got to continue with that communication and keep that chemistry going."
Through three and a half seasons, the Iowa State product has recorded 23.5 sacks, including 18.5 over the last two years alone. Still, the Jets want more, and McDonald's slow start to the 2026 season isn't helping matters .
Through five games, McDonald has recorded two sacks and 12 pressures , according to Pro Football Focus . He is receiving more snaps due to injuries, but hasn't made the kind of impact that other players around him have.
And he knows that has to change.
The numbers aren't necessarily bad for McDonald over five games. PFF has graded him as the 40th-best edge rusher in the sport out of 106 players. That puts him in an above-average grade.
After being considered one of the worst run defenders in the league last year, the 27-year-old has improved significantly in that area as well, ranking 72nd at his position. Good? Definitely not, but improved nevertheless.
More importantly, though, McDonald's work has caught the eye of head coach Aaron Glenn over the last several weeks.
"(Will) was effective in a number of jobs that we had him do," Jets head coach Aaron Glenn said. "I think you guys probably saw that he was really the spy on Deshaun (Watson), and he made a number of plays from running him down and making a tackle on the quarterback, because he has that ability to be able to do that. Another thing that you guys might not have picked up on: he was on the kickoff team, and he did a hell of a job."
McDonald knows the start of the season may not have been as successful as he probably would have wanted. His pressures and sack totals will all need an uptick if he wants to secure a lengthy contract extension after the season.
But if the pressure is beginning to mount, the fourth-year edge rusher isn't showing it. Instead, he shared a perspective exclusively with Sports Illustrated on Friday that should ease fans' concerns.
McDonald is right. He still has 12 games left in the season, and he has a history of getting sacks in bunches. While he only recorded eight last year, four came in one game—a 27-20 win over the Browns last November.
Eventually, the sacks will need to come. In fact, Sunday against the Patriots seems like the perfect time to get a bunch.
No Jets edge rusher tandem has ever recorded 10 sacks in a single season together. The closest came in the early 2000s, when John Abraham and Shaun Ellis actually recorded 10-plus sacks in opposite years between 2002 and 2005.
Yet despite his slow start in the sack department, McDonald believes he and second-overall pick David Bailey will hit that total by the end of 2026.
McDonald was once in Bailey's shoes. As a former first-round pick, the Iowa State product became the first edge rusher in over a decade to record a 10-sack season in 2024. But after a down year in 2025 and just two sacks to begin this year, most people's attention has turned to Bailey.
Especially after a three-sack performance (h/t NFL) against the Browns last week.
THIRD sack of the day for David Bailey @CLEvsNYJ on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/QTqQqo79NN
McDonald isn't worried about sharing the limelight with the top pick from April, though. During training camp, McDonald was seen working off to the side and teaching Bailey key footwork drills that would aid the rookie throughout 2026. So far, that extra tutelage has worked, even if the veteran edge rusher has seen something different from Bailey to begin with.
"I helped him with the techniques and just critiquing everything," McDonald said. "But in terms of, like, athletic ability and, you know, just getting to the ball, getting off, he already has all of that."
In the NFL—especially in the edge rusher world—being a leader isn't enough. Results matter more. If McDonald wants to earn a second contract with the team, his sack totals will need to improve. His run defense, while improved, will also need to take another step.
The Jets believe he will get there. But McDonald knows the time is now to get going.

title: Jets Have 3 Clear Advantages Over Patriots Going into Week 6
full_text:
No one expects the New York Jets to walk into Foxborough this weekend and upset the New England Patriots.
New York is coming off a three-win season while the Patriots are coming off a Super Bowl appearance. The Jets have played inconsistent football to begin the year while New England is on a two-game winning streak.
But stranger things have happened across the NFL. New York has the tools in place to pull off said upset.
And they have an advantage in three key areas to make sure it sticks.
The name of Sunday's game is pressure. It's true that Patriots quarterback Drake Maye is very good against the blitz. That won't matter so long as the Jets are able to get consistent pressure on the young signal-caller with their four downlinemen.
From David Bailey to Will McDonald to Jowon Briggs, New York needs to get pressure throughout Sunday. The good news is that the Patriots offense is still somewhat of a weakness for the team. They are dealing with a number of injuries and while the hobbled group has stayed afloat over the last couple of weeks, there's an advantage here for the Jets to exploit.
If New York gets the kind of rush production they got against Cleveland, it could stymie the entire offensive gameplan for the Patriots.
Christian Gonzalez should be good to go for Sunday's contest. If New England was smart, they would have him travel with Jets star receiver Garrett Wilson throughout the game.
New York needs to consistently feed targets for Wilson throughout Sunday. The best way to do that is by getting him in the slot and in off coverage. So long as the Jets give Wilson space to move, they'll be able to get chunk plays and positive influences across the offense.
Wilson is an ascending talent and someone who seems to be taking the true moniker of a top-10 receiver. Beating up Gonzalez and New England's other corners is just the next step for him going forward.
The Patriots currently sit at 19th in the league in turnovers forced this season. While they can be opportunistic, it just isn't something they are known for this year.
That's a good thing for the Jets offense, even without some of their key players in the game. Geno Smith has yet to throw an interception this season, and has played very well compared to last year's struggles with the Las Vegas Raiders.
If New York doesn't turn the ball offensively, it will give them an edge, especially since the Patriots have a quarterback tied for the league-lead in interceptions so far this season.
Winning the turnover battle is more important than ever in a game like this.

title: Joseph Ossai Is Becoming a Bigger Jets Offseason Regret With Each Passing Week
full_text:
After beating the Browns 17-12 last Sunday, the New York Jets enter Week 6 looking to accomplish something they haven’t done since 2023: win consecutive games.
This won’t be easy, as the Jets face the Patriots in the team’s first divisional showdown of the season. New England, led by quarterback Drake Maye, has been red-hot over the past two weeks. However, if Gang Green wins these three matchups, they could leave Gillette Stadium with a victory.
Unfortunately, the Jets will have to do so without a few of their key players, including edge rusher Joseph Ossai. Head coach Aaron Glenn ruled the five-year veteran from Texas out on Friday after Ossai missed Wednesday and Thursday’s practices with an ankle injury he suffered against Cleveland (h/t Rich Cimini).
Out for Sunday: Breece Hall, Adonai Mitchell, Joseph Ossai and Dylan Parham. Kenyon Sadiq will be full practice today and is finishing his concussion protocol, per Glenn. #Jets
Ossai has appeared in just three of the Jets’ six games this season. He previously dealt with a plantar fascia issue, which forced him to miss the first two contests this season.
In the games he's played, Ossai has been underwhelming, recording nine tackles, seven of them in one game, and zero pressures in 107 defensive snaps.
Although it’s still early, the Ossai signing is already starting to look like a questionable move by the Jets’ brass.
After giving up the fourth-most rushing yards (139.5) and recording the second-fewest sacks last season, upgrading the defensive line was one of New York’s top offseason priorities.
GM Darren Mougey brought in Ossai to help address these needs, signing the former Bengal to a three-year, $34.5 million contract.
The 26-year-old came off his best season with Cincinnati, registering 43 total tackles, five sacks, and 43 pressures. While Ossai displayed potential as a pass rusher, the Jets primarily brought him in to strengthen their run defense.
Last season, Ossai recorded 13 stops and earned a 70.7 run-defense grade, per Pro Football Focus, ranking 25th among 115 qualifying edge rushers.
With New York, he’s been ineffective as a pass rusher and against the run, earning a 50.9 pass-rush grade and a 54.3 run-defense grade, struggling in both areas despite limited playing time.
Ossai still has plenty of time to turn things around, but it’s hard to feel optimistic when other edge rushers whom the Jets could’ve signed are playing important roles for their respective teams.
Derick Hall and Dre’Mont Jones signed contracts in a similar price range and have been playing well so far.
Hall, who re-signed with the Seahawks on a three-year, $42 million contract, has been a reliable rotational contributor, recording 13 total tackles, two sacks, 13 pressures, and three stops. Although his production hasn’t drawn as much attention as other players on Seattle’s talented defensive line, Hall has been a quality contributor.
Jones, meanwhile, signed a three-year, $36.5 million contract with the Patriots and has emerged as a key contributor. Jones has been the team’s best player against the run, per PFF , earning a 77.6, which ranks 11th among 106 qualifying edge rushers. He’s also been an impactful addition to New England’s pass rush, tying for second on the team in pressure with 14.
With Glenn listing Ossai as week-to-week and Braiden McGregor out for the season, New York could start giving Nate Lynn some reps . The former undrafted free agent was a preseason standout, recording eight total tackles and three sacks in two games.
However, if the Jets pull off an upset against the Patriots, they could explore the trade market to bolster the defensive line. Improving to 3-3 would give New York more incentive to invest in its playoff chances, whereas it would be less inclined to surrender a draft pick if they drop to 2-4.
Regardless of how they address their immediate needs, moving on from Ossai won’t be something they do, even if his play doesn’t improve. After this season, his cap hit jumps from $5.46 million to $12.25 million in 2027, per Spotrac , while releasing him before June 1 would cost the team $17.25 million in dead cap.
For now, New York will hope Ossai can return to the field soon and start playing at the level of his contract.

title: Jets Trade Deadline Big Board: Realistic Targets, Possible Sells, & More
full_text:
At 2-3, it's still too early to determine if the Jets intend to be buyers or sellers ahead of November's NFL trade deadline. Much can change over the next month.
But as we get closer to the Nov. 10 deadline, the team's improved play could help the organization push to be more aggressive going forward. Whether that means accumulating more draft capital or acquiring proven talent is up to the outcomes of the coming games.
With that, it's time to break down players the Jets could target in a potential deadline deal, as well as those Gang Green could ship out if the bottom falls out .
Here are the list of opponents the Jets will face between now and the trade deadline next month
A 2-2 mark would put the organization at 4-5 and well on its way to a significantly improved record from the year before. If the Jets reach that mark, then that could be the perfect sign for general manager Darren Mougey to make a move.
New York has big needs along the defensive line, including tackle, edge rusher, and even at linebacker. There should be plenty of names that fit that mold.
For whom, though? Here are some realistic targets the Jets could look at:
If the bottom falls out for the Eagles with so many injuries , they could look to trade away assets that they know they won't be able to retain. After extending Jordan Davis and Jalen Carter, it's clear that the Eagles see Ojomo as the odd man out.
Ojomo could see a contract similar to the one Milton Williams got from the Patriots (four years, $104 million, per Spotrac ). He's an ascending young player with plenty of upside. New York may have to give up a third-round pick, but it would be worth it to help bring in a plug-and-play starter on their defensive line.
Daron Payne, DT (Commanders)
It's a similar situation with Commanders tackle Daron Payne. The former Pro Bowler could be moved if Washington continues to lose, and that could lead the Jets to bring in another veteran presence for their defensive line.
Remember, David Onyemata has been lost for most of the season after dealing with core muscle surgery. New York has missed both his veteran presence and his ability to stop the run, two things Payne could actually help with.
Given his age (29), Payne probably cost even less compared to a young player like Ojomo.
Josh Sweat, OLB (Cardinals)
It's well documented that Josh Sweat wants out of Arizona . It's also well documented that the Jets have a pass rush that needs to improve. Kinglsey Enagbare has been a solid free-agent pickup, but with Joseph Ossai injured again, that leaves a hole in the group.
Acquiring a player like Sweat would give the team a consistent pass rusher who is much better against the run than people realize.
If things fall apart for the Jets over the next month, they could also move on from some players they won't be re-signing during the offseason. Here are a couple of names to keep an eye on:
I've been on record saying the Jets should try everything in their power to extend Dane Belton . For Andre Cisco, though, the veteran is more expendable. New York could get him for a late-round draft selection and still have a solid safety room going into 2027.
Kingsley Enagbare has been a revelation early on his one-year deal with the Jets. He's up to two sacks on the year but has been impactful in every game he has played, recording 12 pressures , according to Pro Football Focus .
Enagbare could be someone the team tries to get a mid-round pick for if they can't rack up a few wins over the coming weeks.
Harrison Phillips is a building block in the eyes of the Jets, but if New York is out of contention again, it may behoove the team to try to get draft capital for the defensive tackle on the open market. Remember, Phillips is a free agent after this year , so he very well may leave the team in a few months anyway.
Getting something for him, especially if the team is noncompetitive over the next few weeks, is a forward-thinking choice.

title: Friday's Jets Practice Notebook: Good Injury News, Eyes on the Pats & More in Week 6
full_text:
FLORHAM PARK, N.J. — You don't need Jets wide receiver Garrett Wilson to tell you how big Sunday's contest against the Patriots is for Gang Green.
A victory moves New York to 3-3 and arguably their most significant win as a franchise in years. A loss wouldn't sink their season, but it would highlight that the team perhaps isn't as far ahead as many fans would have hoped at this point.
Before the team takes the field in Foxborough, though, the Jets had another Friday practice. It's time to open the notebook to see where the organization is heading .
Let's start with the good news on the injury front.
New York is expected to have rookie wide receiver Omar Cooper Jr. back on the field with the team after missing the last few weeks with an ankle injury. Dane Belton, Kenyon Sadiq, and Kiko Mauigoa are all expected to be able to play as well.
For Sadiq, the first-round tight end still needs to pass the next phase of concussion protocol, but there's hope he will in time for Sunday's game.
New York will, however, remain without Breece Hall, Adonai Mitchell, Dylan Parham, and Joseph Ossai, as all have been designated as "week-to-week" according to head coach Aaron Glenn. That said, the coach did say there was some hope that all four players may return to practice next week.
Getting Cooper and Sadiq on the field would be massive for a Jets passing offense that has struggled in recent weeks. At the very least, though, it should give New York a chance to see more of their talented rookie class in action against a tough opponent.
Sunday's contest won't be easy for the Jets. The Patriots have a top-10 defensive unit in almost every category across the board. With Cooper expected to return to the field, New York's passing offense is expected to get a boost.
But that doesn't mean the team is going to be throwing the ball to start against the Jets' arch rival, according to Glenn.
The Jets have not hidden the fact that they want to be a run-first team. That said, it could be seen as a mistake for the team to openly talk about running the football effectively against a Patriots defense that looks for any advantage it can. New England should expect to do everything in their power to stop Gang Green's rushing attack.
Even after a career game from Braelon Allen in last week's win over Cleveland.
"I thought Braelon did a hell of a job," Glenn said of the team's rushing performance. "The whole line and the run concepts that we had... I thought was pretty good."
Right or wrong, the Jets are going to push the run game on Sunday. Time will tell whether being open about it will work.
New York understands that the season is not made or broken by the outcome of Sunday's game. That said, a potential win could fundamentally shift how the team is perceived in the NFL.
Not just as a possible playoff team, but one that seems to be ending the Jets' demons across their division .
Since 2011, the Jets are 25-65 against AFC East opponents. They have beaten the Patriots in Foxborough just once during that stretch. Last season, New York was 0-6 against their biggest rivals in the division.
And while it certainly weighed on fans, a different approach was felt by the team's head coach.
"It was more or less just the season weighed on me. It didn't matter who we lost to," Glenn said. "I don't look at it as more as just division games. I look at it more as just winning games. Because I think at the end of the day, that's what this is all about."
If the Jets are going to prove to the NFL that they are, in fact, improved from the years of struggles they have seen, then winning divisional contests, even against the Patriots, will be massive.
The Jets have been penalized the second most of any other team in the league this season. Some fans point to the team's lack of discipline. Others wonder if this franchise-consistent problem will ever be fixed.
Glenn and the offense, though, have the right mindset. Other teams like the Bills, Seahawks, Ravens, and Packers are all close to the Jets' penalty totals. The difference between the Jets and these playoff contenders is the fact they haven't been able to recover from a mistake.
And that's something the Jets are working on.
Penalties are going to happen in the NFL. Pre-snap and in-game penalties are just things that are dealt to every team. The difference is that good teams are able to recover from a false start or a hold, and bad teams are not.
So far this season, the Jets have been unable to recover whenever a mistake is made. That needs to change going forward.

title: David Bailey's DROY Case Is Undeniable (Here's How the Jets' Rookie Can Pull Away in the Race)
full_text:
As the Jets prepare for their first AFC East opponent of the season, when they face the Patriots on Sunday, all eyes will be on Gang Green to see if they can end a pitiful trend against divisional competition amid a combined 25-65 record dating back to 2011.
To pull off the upset, New York's defense will have a huge say in that, after being the most dominant unit on the field in the 17-12 win over the Browns last Sunday. The Jets combined for eight sacks and clearly went into the game with the intention of loading the box and creating constant pressure on Deshaun Watson, a decision that proved to be the right call by head coach Aaron Glenn .
Someone who was instrumental in that success was rookie EDGE David Bailey, going off for three sacks, seven tackles (five solo), three tackles for loss, and four quarterback hits. That performance led to him earning AFC Defensive Player of the Week honors and well-deserved recognition.
That said, he still has a lot to prove if he truly wants to live up to the No. 2 draft pick.
It was a relatively slow start for Bailey, but he continues to build his Defensive Rookie of the Year case with each passing week, and his breakout against the Browns was a key first step toward winning that award by season's end. His stock is already skyrocketing as New York's best pass rusher, and his Week 5 performance was his first real reminder why.
Bailey has made it clear that he is still adjusting to his role in the NFL , as he has had to adjust to no longer being an every-down pass rusher like he was accustomed to at Texas Tech. While his run defense was an area he needed to improve, Bailey has made strides in that area and has continued to dominate the pass rush (h/t NFL) after leading college football in sacks last season.
David Bailey was a man on a mission in Week 5 🔥 @Pepsi pic.twitter.com/DKOYWjlsLg
According to Pro Football Focus , Bailey has the 43rd-ranked overall grade (68.6) and the 10th-most pressures (20) out of 106 qualified edge defenders in the league. His pass-rush grade (59.5) is 69th, but most impressively, his run-defense grade (76.1) is 16th for a player who has been a pleasant surprise in that particular area. In fact, that grade is even higher than fifth overall pick Arvell Reese (74.0), who was already expected to become a three-down defender for the Giants.
So far, Bailey is averaging four pressures per game, putting him on pace for 68—including a season-high nine vs. the Browns. For reference, he finished with 39 or fewer in each of his three years at Stanford before racking up 81 in his lone campaign at Texas Tech.
There is no doubt that Bailey has been the best rookie on this Jets team so far , and he appears to only be getting started with his high motor and explosiveness off the snap that make him so hard to defend.
Looking at the upcoming schedule, everything is in front of Bailey to compete for the DROY award, especially as certain sportsbooks are beginning to favor him over the likes of fellow defenders Reese and Dolphins linebacker Jacob Rodriguez.
As of Friday afternoon, DraftKings Sportsbook lists Bailey as the current favorite to be named DROY (+200) over Reese (+300) and Rodriguez (+350). With Commanders LB Sonny Styles (+1000) the only other player with odds better than +2000, it looks like a three-man race unless something changes between now and January.
While Rodriguez (57) and Reese (43) have more total tackles than Bailey (25) so far, they have only one sack combined. Granted, they both have an interception through the first five games as well, but neither has had the same overall impact in pass rush as Bailey has up to this point.
Look no further than Sunday's road trip to Gillette Stadium for Bailey's next opportunity to improve his case for the DROY award. The Patriots are banged up on the offensive line, including the questionable status of starting left tackle Will Campbell (right knee). Combine that with QB Drake Maye's turnover-prone start to the 2026 season, and there is every reason to believe that Bailey can be just as impactful again this weekend.
After that, the Jets return home for two games against the winless Dolphins and the surprising Raiders. Both QBs—Malik Willis and Kirk Cousins—have combined for eight interceptions and have been sacked 22 times. In other words, Bailey has an opportunity to cement his frontrunner status in the next three games before a two-game stretch against the Chiefs and Bills ensues.
Bailey made a strong statement against the Browns and showed that the 2026 Defensive Rookie of the Year Award starts and stops with him. If he keeps performing at (or even improves on) his current level and makes a major impact on the field, Bailey could pull away in this race and prove the Jets made the right decision when they selected him second overall in April.

title: 3 Key Matchups Will Decide Jets’ Week 6 Outcome vs. Patriots (Gang Green Needs a Braelon Allen Encore)
full_text:
The Jets head into Week 6 trying to build on last week’s victory over the Browns. This will be a challenge, however, as they’ll be heading to Gillette Stadium to take on the Patriots.
Even with the Tom Brady-Bill Belichick era behind them, the Patriots continue to dominate this rivalry, with New York going 2-10 against New England since 2020. Although leaving with a win will be difficult, especially with the Patriots turning things around in the last two games, it’s not impossible.
If Gang Green can win these three matchups, they’ll give themselves a chance to pull off a road upset and earn back-to-back victories for the first time since 2023.
Unlike last year, the Jets have been ineffective at running the ball, ranking 22nd in rushing yards per game (94) and tied for 25th in yards per attempt (3.6). Despite their inefficiencies, their victories have relied heavily on pounding the ball.
In their three losses, the Jets ran the ball on 31.3%, 37.5%, and 43.8% of their plays, averaging 61.3 rushing yards per game. In their two victories, however, they ran the ball on 48.5% and 62% of their plays, averaging 143 rushing yards per game.
This trend makes establishing the run a priority against the Patriots, even without Breece Hall, who’s missed the team’s last three practices before officially being ruled out by the Jets on Friday, reported by ESPN 's Rich Cimini.
Out for Sunday: Breece Hall, Adonai Mitchell, Joseph Ossai and Dylan Parham. Kenyon Sadiq will be full practice today and is finishing his concussion protocol, per Glenn. #Jets
Braelon Allen will likely take on the bulk of the workload again . Allen played a key role in the Jets' Week 5 win over the Browns, setting career highs in rushing attempts (24) and rushing yards (116) and adding a touchdown.
Running the ball won’t be easy against the Patriots' defense, as they rank sixth in rushing yards allowed per game (90.8) and are tied for 13th in yards per carry allowed (4). Still, the Jets can’t afford to abandon the ground game if they struggle to find success early.
Pounding the football will be crucial to taking pressure off Geno Smith and giving the Patriots another dimension to keep New England’s defense guessing. With Garrett Wilson being the team’s only reliable receiving option, maintaining a balanced attack will be crucial.
The more the New York feeds Allen, the more opportunities he will have to break through for explosive runs. That’s exactly what happened last week against the Brown, as the bruising back from Wisconsin displayed his big-play potential, recording five runs of 10 or more yards.
If the Jets remain patient and continue feeding him the ball, Allen could eventually break through for a big gain. Although the Jets' offensive line hasn’t been great at creating running lanes, ranking 14th in run blocking , per Pro Football Focus, one play can spark the ground game.
At 6'1" and 250 lbs, Allen has the size that makes him hard to bring down and the speed to break away from defenders. If New York’s offensive line opens running lanes for him at the second level, Allen could replicate similar success on the ground and keep New England’s defense on its heels.
Two weeks ago, this matchup looked more attainable for the Jets, with Drake Maye struggling mightily through the first three weeks. The third-year quarterback from North Carolina threw for 585 yards, one touchdown, and six interceptions in New England’s first three games.
But in the last two games, Maye has started to look like the MVP runner-up he was last season, throwing for 643 yards, seven passing touchdowns, and just one interception. He’s also remained elite against the blitz, completing 71.7% of his passes, throwing four touchdowns and an interception.
To limit Maye success through the air, New York must make some adjustments to its scheme.
With head coach Aaron Glenn taking over as defensive play caller, the Jets have taken an aggressive approach, ranking fourth in blitz rate at 39%. They’ll have to switch things up against Maye and rely on their front four to generate pressure rather than consistently sending extra rushers.
Maye has been far less effective when defenses don’t blitz, completing 62.9% of his passes for one touchdown and six interceptions. When defenses sit back, he can hold the ball too long while searching for big plays, leading to costly mistakes and 14 sacks.
This puts added pressure on the Jets’ secondary to stay disciplined in coverage and limit downfield opportunities, where Maye is most dangerous. With A.J. Brown potentially making his return, Gang Green could face an even greater challenge downfield.
New York can match Brown’s physicality with Azareye’h Thomas, who’s impressed in coverage this year, earning a 74.4 coverage grade, per PFF , ranking 11th among 104 qualifying cornerbacks .
Ultimately, the Jets’ ability to contain Maye will depend on how their secondary plays in coverage. If New York can prevent the Patriots’ receivers from creating separation, it could force Maye to hold onto the ball long enough for the pass rush to get to him.
Staying with Brown and the Patriots’ other deep threats could also create interceptions, which they’ll need to stay in the game.
For the most part, Smith has been a good game-managing quarterback. The 14-year veteran impressed with his efficiency in the first three games, completing 75.5% of his passes for 783 yards, four touchdowns, and zero interceptions.
While Smith kept the ball out of harm’s way in the last two games, he hasn’t been as effective, completing 55.5% of his passes for 301 yards and two touchdowns. Although injuries to several key playmakers have played a role, Smith has been less aggressive in pushing the ball downfield, attempting just 12 passes of 20 yards or more this season.
However, Smith’s struggles aren’t entirely on him. Aside from Wilson, the rest of the Jets’ receiving corps has struggled to get open , forcing Smith to wait for throwing windows to develop. He’s tied 14th in time to throw at 2.93 seconds and has been sacked 16 times through five games, the third-most in the league.
This is where New England’s pass rush could make life miserable for Smith. The Patriots rank ninth in blitz percentage (36.1%) and are tied for 15th in quarterback pressure rate (36.7%), according to NFL Next Gen Stats.
Although their pass rush hasn’t been as effective, with New England tying for 12th in sacks with 11, defensive coordinator Zak Kuhr could test Smith early by dialing up some blitzes.
If the Jets want to improve their chances of winning, Smith must make quick decisions with the ball and avoid holding the ball too long. Screen and quick passes to Isaiah Williams and,if he plays,  Kenyon Sadiq could help counter the Patriots’ blitzes and give the offense opportunities to move the chains.
Smith must also continue to target Wilson early and often. Reich must build on last week’s game plan against the Browns and get Wilson more involved in the slot. The five-year veteran made plays with the ball in his hands last week, recording a season-high 55 yards after the catch.
Even if cornerback Christian Gonzalez plays and lines up against him, Smith shouldn’t shy away from targeting his best playmaker. Getting Wilson the ball in space rather than relying on him to make contested catches downfield could help New York move the ball downfield.
